items.title: Anonymous organization-level registries for Dependabot
items.lede: You can now select Anonymous as the authentication method for an organization-level private registry. Use it for registries that Dependabot can reach without credentials, such as an internal package mirror that allows anonymous reads.
items.text:
You can now select Anonymous as the authentication method for an organization-level private registry. Use it for registries that Dependabot can reach without credentials, such as an internal package mirror that allows anonymous reads.

On github.com, Dependabot update jobs can only reach hosts on the egress allowlist and the private registries you configure. A private registry that’s only defined in a file such as .npmrc or nuget.config is blocked. Organization-level registries apply to every repository you grant access to, including repositories that only use Dependabot security updates and don’t have a dependabot.yml file.

To add a registry, go to your organization’s Settings, select Secrets and variables, then Private registries, and choose New private registry. If you used a placeholder token as a workaround, delete that registry and add it again with Anonymous authentication. This is necessary because you can’t change the authentication method of an existing registry.

The Anonymous option is now generally available on github.com and will be available in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Learn more about giving security features access to private registries and resolving a blocked host in a Dependabot update job.

links.text: giving security features access to private registries
resolving a blocked host in a Dependabot update job

items.title: Push attribution for commits in limited public preview
items.lede: GitHub now durably records the authenticated user who pushed each commit and surfaces that pusher identity in the UI and API alongside the existing author and committer fields.
items.text:
GitHub now durably records the authenticated user who pushed each commit and surfaces that pusher identity in the UI and API alongside the existing author and committer fields.

Commit author and committer fields are just strings that the pushing client supplies, so anyone with write access to a repository can set them to any name and email they choose. That makes it possible for an attacker who compromises a low-privilege account to forge commits that appear to come from a trusted maintainer, evading review policies and confusing audit trails. GitHub already authenticates pushes. This release adds durable, per-commit pusher attribution alongside the author and committer metadata.

With this release:

- Every commit pushed to a repository now has a durable, authenticated pusher identity attached to it, independent of whatever the author and committer metadata claims.

- A new repository rule condition, Committer must match pusher, blocks pushes where the committer metadata doesn’t match any verified email address of the authenticated pusher. This closes a path for commit identity spoofing.

You can use the pusher identity to spot-check suspicious activity or speed up security investigations instead of relying on unverified metadata. You can do this because the pusher identity is now visible wherever commits are shown instead. To enforce stricter identity requirements on a repository, add the new Committer must match pusher rule to a ruleset.

Push attribution is available now as a limited public preview for GitHub Enterprise customers. If you are interested in joining the preview, please contact your account team and request access.

Learn more about configuring push rulesets.

items.title: Client telemetry user attribution and configurable capture
items.lede: Enterprise administrators can now use telemetry in managed settings to attribute GitHub Copilot activity to a user without collecting their prompts, responses, or tool content.
items.text:
Enterprise administrators can now use telemetry in managed settings to attribute GitHub Copilot activity to a user without collecting their prompts, responses, or tool content.

The telemetry.capture.identity setting adds three attributes to OpenTelemetry (OTel) data:

- user.name: The authenticated Copilot account name, currently the GitHub login.

- process.user.name: The local operating-system account.

- host.name: The local machine name.

Identity capture is off by default and remains separate from the existing pseudonymous user identifier. Fine-grained capture controls are available in Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and VS Code sessions using Agent Host.

Administrators can also independently control five additional capture classes:

- prompts: User, system, and developer prompts and supported input context.

- responses: Assistant responses and supported reasoning content.

- toolArguments: Raw tool arguments, commands, tool schemas, and identifiers for tools, MCP servers, plugins, and hooks.

- toolOutput: Tool results and execution-error details.

- policyDetail: Raw policy details such as sandbox filesystem paths.

Every capture class is off by default. Explicit managed values take precedence over local settings, SDK configuration, and environment variables. The existing captureContent setting remains available as a legacy shorthand for the five content classes, but it never enables identity.

Prompt, tool, and policy capture can include source code, file contents, commands, tool results, and workspace or user-profile paths. Enable only the classes required for your audit use case and send them to an approved collection endpoint.

To learn more, see the enterprise managed settings reference and monitor agent usage with OpenTelemetry.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

items.title: Improved detection for withdrawn Dependabot alerts
items.lede: You can now more easily detect withdrawn Dependabot alerts. Dependabot withdraws and removes an alert when the advisory or vulnerability that produced it is no longer valid. Two changes help you detect these withdrawals:
items.text:
You can now more easily detect withdrawn Dependabot alerts. Dependabot withdraws and removes an alert when the advisory or vulnerability that produced it is no longer valid. Two changes help you detect these withdrawals:

- Webhooks: The dependabot_alert webhook event now includes a withdrawn action. The payload contains identifiers captured before the alert was removed, such as the alert number, GHSA and CVE IDs, package, and manifest path. If you already subscribe to dependabot_alert events, you’ll automatically receive these deliveries.

- REST API: Requests to get or update a withdrawn alert now return 410 Gone instead of 404 Not Found, so you can tell a withdrawn alert apart from one that never existed.

These changes are available for all repositories on github.com and will be included in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Learn more about the dependabot_alert webhook event and the REST API endpoints for Dependabot alerts.

links.text: REST API endpoints for Dependabot alerts

items.title: Enterprise managed settings enforcement updates
items.lede: Enterprise administrators can now require supported GitHub Copilot clients to retrieve current server-managed settings at startup instead of relying on a cached policy. We are also adding minimum client version requirements to governance-focused managed settings keys over time, starting with the sandbox key.
items.text:
Enterprise administrators can now require supported GitHub Copilot clients to retrieve current server-managed settings at startup instead of relying on a cached policy. We are also adding minimum client version requirements to governance-focused managed settings keys over time, starting with the sandbox key.

Force refresh settings on client startup

Set forceRemoteSettingsRefresh to true through server-managed, MDM-managed, or file-based settings when a policy change must take effect before Copilot starts. The setting is supported in Copilot CLI, VS Code, and the GitHub Copilot app.

MDM-managed and file-based delivery can require freshness before the client signs in for the first time. A server-managed value begins requiring refreshes on subsequent startups after the client has received it once. While the setting is active, a cached response cannot satisfy the freshness requirement. If the client cannot confirm current policy, it fails closed rather than running with a stale or unconfirmed policy. Without this setting, clients continue to use the normal managed-settings cache for faster startup and resilience during transient service failures.

Minimum required client version

We’ve also added enforcement of a required minimum client version to the sandbox key in support of the generally available local sandbox capability. When this key is included in managed settings, users who pin to older versions of Copilot clients will now be forced to update in order to resume using Copilot.

To learn more, see Deploying enterprise managed settings.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

items.title: Search and filter for budgets now available
items.lede: The “Budgets and alerts” page in your GitHub billing settings now shows all of your budgets in one list that you can search and filter. Whether you manage budgets for a personal account, enterprise or organization, you can find a specific budget without paginating through the full list.
items.text:
The “Budgets and alerts” page in your GitHub billing settings now shows all of your budgets in one list that you can search and filter. Whether you manage budgets for a personal account, enterprise or organization, you can find a specific budget without paginating through the full list.

With this release, you can:

- Search or filter budgets by scope, product, or SKU. In enterprises and organizations, you can also search by user.

- Narrow the list to one scope, such as organizations or cost centers, from the Scope menu.

- Track user-level budgets in the same list, including which budget applies to a specific user.

To learn more, see Setting up budgets.

items.title: Code scanning AI Scan metrics in security overview
items.lede: Organization and enterprise administrators can now observe the impact of AI Scan for pull requests in security overview. New metrics show how many AI Scan findings were generated, resolved, the remediation rate, which repositories generated findings, trends over the selected reporting period, and how often developers…
items.text:
Organization and enterprise administrators can now observe the impact of AI Scan for pull requests in security overview. New metrics show how many AI Scan findings were generated, resolved, the remediation rate, which repositories generated findings, trends over the selected reporting period, and how often developers applied autofix suggestions.

The “CodeQL pull requests” page is now named “Code scanning on pull requests” and includes separate CodeQL and AI Scan tabs. The AI Scan tab shows total findings and how many findings include or do not include an autofix suggestion. Metrics from the “CodeQL pull requests” page are now under the CodeQL tab.

These metrics help security teams evaluate the effectiveness of AI Scan across their organization or enterprise, understand developer response, and make informed rollout and investment decisions without reviewing individual pull requests.

This public preview is available on github.com, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud, for customers with GitHub Code Security or GitHub Advanced Security. GitHub Enterprise Server isn’t supported for this release.

Learn more about AI Scan for pull requests and join the AI Scan Community discussion.

items.title: Secret scanning blocks Anthropic keys by default, adds Salesforce
items.lede: Secret scanning now detects new secret types from Salesforce, Anthropic, and Cloudsmith, with the new Anthropic secret types blocked with push protection by default.
items.text:
Secret scanning now detects new secret types from Salesforce, Anthropic, and Cloudsmith, with the new Anthropic secret types blocked with push protection by default.

New secret scanning partner

Salesforce is now a secret scanning partner.

When a provider’s secret is found in a public repository, GitHub forwards it to the relevant partner so they can revoke or rotate the credential before it can be abused.

Detectors added

items.title: Audit GitHub Code Quality finding dismissals and reopenings
items.lede: You can now review manual dismissals and reopenings of GitHub Code Quality findings in your organization or enterprise audit log. Findings may appear in either your repository’s default-branch backlog or pull requests. Two new events record these actions:
items.text:
You can now review manual dismissals and reopenings of GitHub Code Quality findings in your organization or enterprise audit log. Findings may appear in either your repository’s default-branch backlog or pull requests. Two new events record these actions:

- repo.code_quality_findings_dismissed records a dismissal of one or more backlog findings.

- repo.code_quality_findings_reopened records a reopening of one or more backlog findings.

Each event includes who made the request, when it happened, the repository and rule, and the identifiers and count of the affected findings.

For repositories with Code Quality enabled, you don’t need additional setup. If you have access to your organization audit log or enterprise audit log, filter by these action names to review activity. On GitHub Enterprise Cloud, you can also retrieve these events through the audit log API.

This improvement is generally available on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including enterprises with data residency. It isn’t available on GitHub Enterprise Server. For more on managing findings, see Fixing code quality findings in your repository backlog.

Join the GitHub Community discussion.

links.text: Fixing code quality findings in your repository backlog

In early testing, Gemini 4 Argon solved more tasks than previous Gemini models on every coding benchmark, with its largest gains in Copilot CLI.
items.text:
Gemini 4 Argon, Google’s newest frontier model, is now generally available in GitHub Copilot. It is designed for complex coding, agentic, and reasoning tasks. items.title: GitHub App improvements for least privilege and management
items.lede: We’re releasing several GitHub Apps improvements today that help developers move off of classic PATs, improve GitHub App management, and request fewer sensitive permissions. We’ve also made it easier for repository administrators to use apps that their administrators have approved and updated the GitHub App credential…
items.text:
We’re releasing several GitHub Apps improvements today that help developers move off of classic PATs, improve GitHub App management, and request fewer sensitive permissions. We’ve also made it easier for repository administrators to use apps that their administrators have approved and updated the GitHub App credential management UI in advance of our planned workload federation features.

New repository creation and installation management permissions

Two new repository fine-grained permissions have been added, available to both fine-grained PATs and GitHub Apps.

- repository_creation:write: Allows the caller to create a repository in the account where it’s granted.

- installation_repositories: write: Allows the caller to add or remove that repository from an installation in the organization.

Create a repository without repository_administration

You can now use the repository_creation:write permission to create repositories without needing the broader repository_administration:write permission.

Previously, an app or PAT needed repository_administration:write to create a repository. That permission also grants other repository administration features like deletion and transfer. This could lead to administrators rejecting apps, banning PATs with this permission, or having to accept the over-privilege risk.

The new permission supports a least-privilege approach by granting only the ability to create repositories. When the repository is created, the app or user that created it will be given access to it. An app using this permission still requires an organization administrator to install the app.

See the API docs for repository creation in organizations, from a template, for the current user, with a fork, and via GraphQL.

Manage installation repositories with an app or fine-grained PAT

The Add a repository to an installation organization-level API and its corresponding removal API now support GitHub Apps and fine-grained PATs. Previously, these APIs only supported the coarse-grained repo scope.

These APIs support a new repository-level fine-grained permission:installation_repositories:write. Having this permission on a repository allows the caller to add or remove that repository from any installation in the organization. If the caller is a user, they must also be an organization owner or an administrator on the repository in question.

This allows organizations to build automation that controls which repositories are accessible to which GitHub Apps without relying on an administrator’s PAT with broad permissions.

Repository administrators can more easily add approved GitHub Apps to repositories

Historically, all apps that requested organization-level access were blocked from being installed on a repository by a repository administrator, no matter what. This restriction has been relaxed in the case where the app is already installed in the organization, meaning it’s been approved by an organization owner for that organization-level access. Repository administrators can now edit an existing installation to add their repositories to an app without requiring organization owner approval. The apps already have the organization-level access, so adding them to another repository in the organization doesn’t increase that access or give the repository administrator additional privileges.

With the addition of the repository_creation permission above, there are now three sensitive permission sets that require organization owner approval:

- All organization-level permissions

- Repository administration

- Repository creation

This change allows repository administrators to better use apps that are already approved for use in their organization.

If you’d like to prevent repository administrators from adding apps to their repositories, see “Restricting GitHub App Installation to Organization Owners” in the docs. For more details on adding an app to a repository, see “Installing a GitHub App“.

Use offline_access with GitHub Apps to gradually reenable short-lived, rotating tokens

GitHub Apps now support the offline_access scope, like OAuth apps.

links.text: Add a repository to an installation organization-level API
Restricting GitHub App Installation to Organization Owners

items.title: GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles in public preview
items.lede: GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles are now in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. Tags and branches can move after you review a workflow, so a later run might execute different code.
items.text:
GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles are now in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. Tags and branches can move after you review a workflow, so a later run might execute different code. Lockfiles let you keep those references in your workflow while running the exact commits you locked.

Editor’s note (October 14th, 2026): Updated which plans have access to this public preview.

If an action is compromised, a moved tag or branch can introduce malicious code into your workflow without a change to your repository. Lockfiles help protect against unexpected dependency changes by keeping workflow runs tied to the commits you locked. Locking does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe, so review dependencies before locking them.

Install the gh actions-lock extension for the GitHub CLI to create and maintain your workflow lockfile. With the extension, you can:

- Pin your dependencies: Generate .github/workflows/actions.lock with reviewable commits for actions and their transitive dependencies.

- Adopt locking gradually: Onboard workflows individually. Once onboarded, a workflow must have lockfile entries for its dependencies, and GitHub Actions runs the recorded commits.

- Keep workflow runs consistent: GitHub Actions requires each dependency of an onboarded workflow to be in the lockfile and uses its recorded commit, even if a tag or branch moves.

- Check for stale lockfiles: Verify that the lockfile is up to date without modifying files, including in a CI check.

The Require lockfile policy is also available in public preview. Enterprise, organization, and repository administrators can require workflows to use lockfiles across their enterprise, organization, or repository.

Keep locked dependencies up to date with Dependabot

Dependabot helps you keep your GitHub Actions dependencies up to date. When it opens a version update for an action in a workflow that is already onboarded, it also regenerates the matching lockfile entry in the same pull request, keeping the updated workflow reference and its locked commit in sync without additional configuration. Read more about Dependabot updates for actions.

Get started

To get started, install the extension from the public gh-actions-lock repository, then review and commit the generated lockfile and workflow changes.

For more details and links to setup instructions, see workflow dependency lockfiles in GitHub Docs.

Share feedback in the existing community discussion or open an issue in the gh-actions-lock repository.

Thank you to the community members who helped shape this preview through testing and feedback, with special thanks to Andrew Nesbitt, François Proulx, Jesse Houwing, and William Woodruff for their close collaboration and iteration on this solution over the past year.

items.title: HydraFusion updates and new Max option
items.lede: HydraFusion has an updated model pool, improved orchestration workflows, and introduces HydraFusion Max. Both HydraFusion and HydraFusion Max are available across VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, and GitHub Copilot CLI and remain in research preview.
items.text:
HydraFusion has an updated model pool, improved orchestration workflows, and introduces HydraFusion Max. Both HydraFusion and HydraFusion Max are available across VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, and GitHub Copilot CLI and remain in research preview.

HydraFusion orchestrates multiple models to produce a single response, bringing together their strengths so you don’t have to choose an individual model for each task.

What’s new in HydraFusion

- Latest frontier models: HydraFusion and HydraFusion Max draw from a pool that now includes Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Luna. The models used for each task vary based on the orchestration workflow.

- Reasoning effort tailored to each step: Previously, HydraFusion only used each model’s default reasoning effort. With this update, it explicitly tailors effort to each stage, using medium effort for initial drafts and high effort for review. This keeps drafting efficient while dedicating deeper reasoning to checking and improving the work.

- Optimized Cascade and Critique workflows:

- Cascade: Previously used an initial model to solve the task, with escalation to a stronger model when needed. It can now include a judging step that inspects the initial work and requests a repair only when needed.

- Critique: Previously relied heavily on text summaries. It now relies more on tools to inspect the actual workspace directly. Critique now also uses parallel critic models to inspect work.

Introducing HydraFusion Max

HydraFusion Max is built on the same architecture and uses the same workflow techniques as HydraFusion, but is tuned for frontier capability on more demanding tasks. It applies higher reasoning efforts where depth and thoroughness matter most, while still using orchestration to consider token efficiency.

Option |
Description |
Typical use case |

HydraFusion |
Balanced approach with moderate token savings. |
Agentic tasks that require a balance of speed, cost, and performance. |

HydraFusion Max |
Frontier capability for more demanding tasks, with token efficiency considered through orchestration. |
Tasks requiring the deepest possible reasoning and most thorough analysis. |

Both options are supported across all three clients, so you can access the latest HydraFusion experience whether you work in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, or the terminal.

HydraFusion and HydraFusion Max are available on Copilot Pro, Pro+, Business, and Enterprise plans with experimental or preview features enabled, subject to your organization’s model policies.

Learn more in the HydraFusion documentation.

Share your feedback in the HydraFusion discussion.

items.title: Email notifications for repository push events have been retired
items.lede: As of October 15, 2026, email notifications for repository push events have been retired and are no longer sent.
items.text:
As of October 15, 2026, email notifications for repository push events have been retired and are no longer sent.

We shut down this feature to help prevent spam and abuse. Because recipients didn’t have to consent before receiving these emails, the feature could be misused to send unwanted messages through GitHub’s email infrastructure.

To continue sending email notifications for repository push events, you can use a GitHub Actions workflow triggered by push events to send emails through your own SMTP server or email provider.

items.title: Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts general availability
items.lede: Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts is now generally available. It remediates alerts by working across your codebase the way a developer would: it explores relevant files, proposes a fix, and reruns CodeQL to confirm the fix closes the alert before opening a pull request for your review.
items.text:
Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts is now generally available. It remediates alerts by working across your codebase the way a developer would: it explores relevant files, proposes a fix, and reruns CodeQL to confirm the fix closes the alert before opening a pull request for your review. Agentic autofix is available to GitHub Code Security and GitHub Advanced Security customers on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

How it works

When you assign a code scanning alert to Copilot, it:

- Explores relevant files across your codebase.

- Generates a proposed fix.

- Validates the fix works by rerunning CodeQL.

- Iterates if needed, then opens a draft pull request ready for your review.

The pull request includes a summary of the fix, why it closes the alert, and the validation steps Copilot took to confirm that it works. When the pull request containing the fix is ready, you can instruct Copilot to make further changes to it by commenting on the pull request or interacting with the session in the Agents tab of your repository.

How to use it

When enabled, agentic autofix replaces the free Generate Fix option on individual code scanning alerts with an Assign to Copilot button.

You can use agentic autofix:

- From any code scanning alert on the repository’s default branch, by assigning the alert to Copilot.

- In the list of security alerts in your repository or security campaign, by selecting up to 25 alerts for Copilot to fix together in a single pull request.

- Via the Update a Code Scanning Alert REST API by setting assignees to ["copilot-swe-agent[bot]"].

Agentic autofix supports code scanning alerts on the repository’s default branch. Alerts detected only on pull requests or other branches cannot be assigned to Copilot.

Access

Agentic autofix requires an enterprise administrator to enable access to it via the new “Agentic autofix” policy in Advanced Security policies.

Once the policy is enabled by an enterprise administrator, an organization or repository administrator can turn on agentic autofix in the Code Security settings for the organization or the repository.

Access also requires a Copilot billing method to be defined.

Billing

Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts consumes AI Credits from your Code Security budget and GitHub Actions minutes. AI Credit usage will be displayed in the “AI usage” section of enterprise billing and licensing as the “Advanced Security” product. You can also set SKU level budgets for Code Security AI credits. Learn more about Copilot usage-based billing.

Learn more

Learn more about agentic autofix in the documentation.

Join the discussion within the GitHub Community.

items.title: AI Scan for pull requests generally available
items.lede: Code scanning AI Scan for pull requests is now generally available. It complements CodeQL by finding vulnerabilities in pull request changes for languages and frameworks that CodeQL does not currently cover, including PHP, Shell/Bash, Terraform configuration (HCL), Dockerfiles, JSP for Java, Blazor for C#, and more.
items.text:
Code scanning AI Scan for pull requests is now generally available. It complements CodeQL by finding vulnerabilities in pull request changes for languages and frameworks that CodeQL does not currently cover, including PHP, Shell/Bash, Terraform configuration (HCL), Dockerfiles, JSP for Java, Blazor for C#, and more.

How it works

AI Scan runs automatically on pull requests when code scanning and the repository’s effective AI Scan setting are enabled. Findings appear alongside CodeQL results on the Conversation and Files changed tabs, with an “AI” indicator to distinguish them from CodeQL alerts. Findings can include an explanation of the security risk and a suggested autofix.

AI Scan findings are advisory. They do not fail the code scanning check and cannot block pull request merges through ruleset requirements. AI Scan does not run on pull requests from forks or pull requests created by Dependabot.

Availability

AI Scan is available for public repositories owned by organizations or personal accounts. For private and internal organization-owned repositories, GitHub Code Security or GitHub Advanced Security is required. A GitHub Copilot license is not required.

Billing

AI Scan for pull requests consumes Code Security AI Credits. AI Credit usage is displayed in the “AI usage” section of enterprise billing and licensing as the “Advanced Security” product. You can also set SKU-level budgets for Code Security AI Credits. Learn more about usage-based billing.

Learn more about AI Scan for pull requests and billing for GitHub Advanced Security AI features.

Join the discussion in the AI Scan Community discussion.

Use the unique committer details to identify where disabling Code Quality could free up licenses for the next billing period without changing your current license charge.

items.title: Multi-repository support and other improvements for GitHub in Slack and Teams
items.lede: @GitHub in Slack and Teams now supports working across multiple repositories in a single conversation. Whether you’re creating issues, opening pull requests, or investigating bugs, you can work across repositories without switching conversations.
items.text:
@GitHub in Slack and Teams now supports working across multiple repositories in a single conversation. Whether you’re creating issues, opening pull requests, or investigating bugs, you can work across repositories without switching conversations.

For example, you can ask @GitHub to:

Create issues from conversations: “@GitHub Create an issue in github/issues to track this bug, using the context from this thread.”

Make code changes: “@GitHub Fix this bug in our frontend repository and open a PR with the changes.”

Track your PRs: “@GitHub Show me all my open PRs across repositories and highlight which ones need my attention.”

Investigate bugs: “@GitHub Investigate this issue using the code in our frontend and backend repositories.”

You can do all of this directly from Slack or Teams, without switching repositories or starting a new conversation.

Additional improvements

We’ve also made several improvements to GitHub in Slack and Microsoft Teams:

More natural conversations: Mention @GitHub anywhere in your message, not just at the beginning.

Smoother repository switching: Move between repositories more easily during a conversation.

Better Slack conversation context: @GitHub can use shared Slack messages and threads as context, making it easier to reference discussions without copying and pasting details.

Improved reliability: We’ve made several improvements to reduce errors, improve task startup, and help @GitHub recover more smoothly from interruptions in Slack and Teams.

Join the discussion within the GitHub Community.

items.text:
You can now use the generally available Xcode 27 runner image to build and test your Apple applications in GitHub Actions. Previously in public preview, this GitHub-hosted image runs on macOS 27 and includes the Xcode 27 toolchain and Apple SDKs.

Xcode-based images

Each image supports one major Xcode version rather than targeting a specific operating system version. This makes it easier to select the toolchain your project needs and know what each runner provides.

Get started

To use the image, set your workflow’s runs-on: value to one of these labels:

- xcode-27

- xcode-27-xlarge

If you already use these labels, you don’t need to change your workflows. The image is available on Apple Silicon (arm64) runners only, not Intel runners.

To view the installed software or report an issue, visit the runner-images repository.

items.title: Open source license compliance generally available
items.lede: Enterprises can now manage their dependencies’ licenses at scale with sophisticated, ruleset-based checks that enforce a centralized policy. Open source license compliance is now generally available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GHEC, for repositories with GitHub Code Security enabled.
items.text:
Enterprises can now manage their dependencies’ licenses at scale with sophisticated, ruleset-based checks that enforce a centralized policy. Open source license compliance is now generally available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GHEC, for repositories with GitHub Code Security enabled.

How it works

Open source license compliance expands on the capabilities of the dependency review action by introducing an enterprise-wide license policy. The policy is activated by targeting repositories with a ruleset that uses a new Require license compliance results before merging condition, similar to the existing code scanning conditions. When developers open pull requests that add or modify dependencies, license checks automatically ensure each new or changed dependency has an acceptable license. The feature annotates the pull request with a message about each noncompliant dependencies. These annotations must be addressed by removing or replacing the dependency, amending the license policy, or creating package exceptions.

Open source license compliance introduces a new predefined enterprise role, Enterprise Open-Source License Manager. Assign this role to individuals or teams who should review and approve closure requests. Policy managers receive email notifications about pending requests and can review them from the enterprise console.

What’s new and improved

Since the public preview release in June, we’ve made several improvements:

- License information is now available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud data residency customers. This not only enables the license compliance feature, but also populates the dependency graph and Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) exports with license data.

- License policy changes now emit audit log events, for integration with external systems of record.

- There are new API endpoints for downloading, updating, and replacing the enterprise license policy.

- There is also a new API endpoint for checking whether packages comply with policy. This enables coding agents to avoid recommending or incorporating packages which violate an organization’s license usage policy.

How to try it

For detailed setup instructions, see About open source license compliance.

For information about API endpoints see REST API endpoints for dependency-graph

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

items.title: Some Git over HTTPS may temporarily require authentication
items.lede: During periods of unusual traffic, GitHub may temporarily require authentication for some clones and fetches of public repositories over HTTPS to help protect github.com’s availability. If an operation is affected, it will fail with a message indicating that authentication is required.
items.text:
During periods of unusual traffic, GitHub may temporarily require authentication for some clones and fetches of public repositories over HTTPS to help protect github.com’s availability. If an operation is affected, it will fail with a message indicating that authentication is required.

To continue, authenticate and retry the operation. You can also wait and retry without authentication after the temporary protection has been lifted.

GitHub applies this protection as narrowly as possible using signals associated with anomalous traffic. Because legitimate and anomalous traffic can sometimes share those signals, legitimate unauthenticated operations may occasionally be affected. This is not a general authentication requirement for public repositories.

The following operations are unaffected:

- Authenticated Git operations over HTTPS

- Git operations over SSH

- Pushes

- Unrelated GitHub web and API traffic

For more reliable automated clones and fetches, configure authentication:

- GitHub Actions: Use the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN.

- Other CI systems: Prefer a GitHub App installation access token. A personal access token can also be used.

- Operations that cannot authenticate: Retry after the temporary protection has been lifted.

This protection applies to repositories on github.com across all plans.

For setup instructions, see about authentication to GitHub and managing remote repositories.

items.title: CodeQL changes for macOS 27, Xcode 27, and Swift 6.4
items.lede: Starting with macOS 27 and Xcode 27, Apple no longer includes Intel (x86_64) code in some of the system binaries and libraries that CodeQL relies on to trace builds. As a result, CodeQL can’t support traced scans on these versions or analyze Swift 6.4.
items.text:
Starting with macOS 27 and Xcode 27, Apple no longer includes Intel (x86_64) code in some of the system binaries and libraries that CodeQL relies on to trace builds. As a result, CodeQL can’t support traced scans on these versions or analyze Swift 6.4.

What’s affected

- Xcode 27: When Xcode 27 is installed, traced extraction isn’t available for C/C++, C#, Go, Java, Kotlin, or Swift.

- macOS 27: Traced extraction may not be available for the previously mentioned languages.

- Swift 6.4: CodeQL doesn’t support Swift 6.4 on any platform.

- Intel-based Macs: CodeQL support for Intel-based Macs will be deprecated in mid-December 2026.

How to keep your scans running

If you scan Swift or use traced builds for other languages, pin your workflows to macOS 26 or earlier and Xcode 26 or earlier. If you use GitHub Actions, pin the runner image and toolchain in your workflow rather than relying on the latest versions.

For C/C++, C#, and Java, you can switch to build mode none, which doesn’t require tracing a build.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

You can now use the REST API to retrieve and update Copilot model policies for enterprises, enterprise teams, agent apps, and organizations.

What’s new

GET and PATCH endpoints are now generally available for model policies at four levels:

- Enterprise: /enterprises/{enterprise}/copilot/model-policies

- Enterprise teams: /enterprises/{enterprise}/teams/{team_slug}/copilot/model-policies

- Agent apps: /enterprises/{enterprise}/copilot/apps/model-policies

Together, these endpoints make it easier to manage Copilot model availability across your enterprise. Enterprise policies can delegate model control to organizations in organization mode, or to teams and apps in enterprise teams mode. items.title: GitHub package firewall in public preview
items.lede: Editor’s note (October 21, 2026): Rewrote the changelog for clarity and added imagery.
items.text:
Editor’s note (October 21, 2026): Rewrote the changelog for clarity and added imagery.

There’s been a recent flood of malware attacks that exploit systems at package installation time. Agents and CI runners are particularly vulnerable to these attacks because they install dependencies to accomplish a task or complete a build without a human in the loop. To stem this tide, GitHub is introducing a new package firewall, which sits between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories. The firewall inspects both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity, acting as an install-time policy gate. The package firewall is available today in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

How it works

First, administrators set policy controls for their enterprise. The controls available today include a configurable cooldown period, checking the GitHub Advisory Database for malware or vulnerability advisories, and supply-chain checks like attestation downgrades.

Then, endpoints like coding agents and CI/CD hosts use the firewall for their requests instead of pointing directly at the upstream package registries. Metadata requests for package lists as well as the actual package downloads flow through the firewall, which evaluates them against the policy. If a package is blocked erroneously, the user can request an exception with a workflow similar to other GitHub Advanced Security features.

Availability and limitations

The package firewall is available in public preview as we scale up the infrastructure behind it and continue to add features based on customer demand. It is available to GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. The service is free while in the preview period. When it reaches general availability, it will be charged based on metered usage, similar to Actions billing.

Currently the package firewall only supports npm packages.

How to use it

For detailed setup instructions, see Protecting endpoints with package firewall. Join the discussion in GitHub Community.

items.title: Dependabot alerts REST API now includes dependency versions
items.lede: You can now get the version of a vulnerable dependency directly from Dependabot alert responses in the REST API. Each alert’s dependency object includes a new version_requirement field with the version or version constraint that Dependabot last recorded for the alert.
items.text:
You can now get the version of a vulnerable dependency directly from Dependabot alert responses in the REST API. Each alert’s dependency object includes a new version_requirement field with the version or version constraint that Dependabot last recorded for the alert.

Alert responses already included the advisory’s vulnerable version range, but not the version in your repository. If you sync alerts to other security tools, you no longer need to parse lockfiles or make a separate GraphQL request for vulnerableRequirements to get that version.

The value depends on how Dependabot detected the dependency:

- Lockfiles: The resolved version.

- Manifests without a lockfile: The version or version constraint declared in the manifest.

- Dependency submission API: The resolved version submitted by your build tooling.

The field is null when no value is available. If an alert covers more than one vulnerable version of a dependency, the field holds one recorded value and may not represent all of them. Long version constraints may also be truncated.

You’ll find version_requirement in responses for individual alerts, in repository, organization, and enterprise alert lists, and in dependabot_alert webhook payloads.

This field is available now on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, and will be included in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Learn more about the REST API endpoints for Dependabot alerts and the dependabot_alert webhook event.

links.text: REST API endpoints for Dependabot alerts

items.title: Updates to GitHub secret scanning
items.lede: This update covers improvements and bug fixes for GitHub secret scanning.
items.text:
This update covers improvements and bug fixes for GitHub secret scanning.

Update to audit log events

On November 12, 2026, the business field in affected secret_scanning_alert.* and secret_scanning_push_protection.bypass audit log events will change from the enterprise display name to the enterprise slug.

To avoid disruption to any automated workflows, you should update integrations that filter by display name before rollout to accept both formats or use business_id instead. The business field remains a string. Event names and numeric business_id values are unchanged.

Recent improvements and bug fixes

- Custom pattern alerts: Existing open alerts stay open when a rescan finds that they still match an edited custom pattern, rather than being closed and reopened.

- Base64-encoded GitHub tokens: In private and internal repositories on github.com with secret scanning enabled, the existing revocation action (public preview) now supports encoded personal access tokens (classic), fine-grained personal access tokens, OAuth access tokens, and GitHub App user access tokens. GitHub automatically decodes the value.

- Dismissal-request webhooks: Payloads now include exemption_request.number, the repository-scoped request number also available in the REST API. Use the repository and request number together to correlate requests across integrations.

- Accessibility: The Request pending status on an alert is now keyboard-focusable without activating an action. The revocation flow announces progress to screen readers and moves focus to its completion panel when that panel appears.

- Bypass-request metadata: Fixed empty secret-type and location details in bypass-request API responses and webhook payloads for command-line pushes when another repository rule ran after secret scanning.

- Delegated bypass: Fixed push failures caused by existing organization-role entries in reviewer lists, and 500 errors when setting valid reviewer configurations for organization-owned repositories through the REST API.

- Custom pattern API: Requests rejected by the scanning service for invalid arguments now return 422 instead of 500, so your integration can distinguish these input errors from server failures.

Learn more

Learn more about enterprise audit log events and the secret scanning REST API. Share your feedback in GitHub Community.

items.title: Bulk migrate branch protections to rulesets for a repository
items.lede: You can now convert all branch protection rules of a repository to rulesets in a single action. This is an extension of the ability to convert a single branch protection rule to a ruleset that we released previously, now allowing for at-scale conversions.
items.text:
You can now convert all branch protection rules of a repository to rulesets in a single action. This is an extension of the ability to convert a single branch protection rule to a ruleset that we released previously, now allowing for at-scale conversions.

How it works

Navigate to Settings → Rulesets in your repository and click Import branch protection rules. In the Review import dialog, you can:

- Preview the rulesets that will be created before you confirm the conversion.

- See which branch protection rules are already covered by an existing ruleset.

- Review cases where one branch protection rule produces multiple rulesets to preserve its original behavior.

- Choose an enforcement status (e.g., Active, Evaluate, or Disabled) and select which rulesets to create.

After you click Create rulesets, choose whether to keep or delete the original branch protection rules.

Why migrate to rulesets?

Rulesets offer several advantages over classic branch protections:

- Apply rules across multiple branches with pattern matching

- Layer multiple rulesets for granular policy control

- Manage rulesets at the organization or enterprise level

- Configure fine-grained bypass permissions for users, teams, and apps

Availability

This feature is available for all repositories where rulesets are available. Learn more about converting your branch protections to repository rulesets.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

links.text: Learn more about converting your branch protections to repository rulesets

items.title: GitHub CLI: Opt in to expiring, auto-refreshing OAuth tokens
items.lede: You can now use expiring, automatically refreshing OAuth credentials in GitHub CLI as part of a public preview. When you opt in, gh stores an expiring access token alongside a rotating refresh token and automatically refreshes the token whenever it is needed.
items.text:
You can now use expiring, automatically refreshing OAuth credentials in GitHub CLI as part of a public preview. When you opt in, gh stores an expiring access token alongside a rotating refresh token and automatically refreshes the token whenever it is needed. You stay authenticated without reauthenticating, and a leaked access token becomes unusable within hours instead of lasting indefinitely.

Opting in at login

Starting with v2.103.0, pass the new --expiring flag when you log in with gh auth login --expiring. To opt in for every sign-in without passing the flag each time, run gh config set expiring_credentials enabled. From then on, there is nothing new to run day to day: gh refreshes the credential for you in the background. To check the state of an expiring credential, including when the current access token expires, run gh auth status.

Using expiring tokens with git

If you authenticate to git over HTTPS and want to use expiring tokens, we strongly recommend configuring gh as your git credential helper by running gh auth setup-git. This lets gh serve and refresh the credential for git, so your expiring token is correctly handled.

We also strongly recommend upgrading to git 2.46 or newer, which lets gh mark expiring credentials so they are not cached past their lifetime. On older git versions, gh still works but prints a one-time recommendation to upgrade.

Good to know

- It’s opt-in and backward compatible. If you don’t opt in through the flag or configuration setting, nothing changes. Existing sign-ins and manually supplied tokens keep working exactly as before.

- You get whatever the server issues. --expiring requests refreshable credentials. If a server does not support them, gh falls back cleanly to a normal nonexpiring token.

- It will become the default over time. Expiring credentials are opt-in today. In a future release, we plan to make them the default for new sign-ins.

Things to watch out for

Expiring access tokens are short-lived, so anything that captures a token once and reuses it later can break. Scripts and extensions that run gh auth token and store the result, or copy the token into another tool, will eventually be left holding an expired token.

If you consume the token outside of gh, read it fresh each time with gh auth token. This refreshes it when needed rather than caching the value. If a workflow depends on a token that stays valid for a long time, hold off on opting in for that workflow. When gh is configured as your git credential helper, it refreshes the credential for you, so git operations over HTTPS keep working.

Who can use it

Expiring tokens are available on github.com and ghe.com today. GitHub Enterprise Server issues them starting with GHES 3.23. On earlier versions, opting in falls back to today’s nonexpiring behavior.

For more on authenticating with GitHub CLI, including expiring tokens, see Authenticating with GitHub CLI.

items.title: Industry comparisons in the Copilot impact dashboard
items.lede: The Copilot impact dashboard now includes an “Industry comparison” section. Enterprises, and organizations that aren’t owned by an enterprise, can compare their Copilot agentic adoption and leverage with aggregated benchmarks from participating peers. Participation is opt-in and disabled by default.
items.text:
The Copilot impact dashboard now includes an “Industry comparison” section. Enterprises, and organizations that aren’t owned by an enterprise, can compare their Copilot agentic adoption and leverage with aggregated benchmarks from participating peers. Participation is opt-in and disabled by default.

What’s new

- Agentic adoption and leverage benchmarks — See the percentage of your users who are agent-first or multi-agent, and how the pull request merge rate of agentic users compares with nonagentic users. Once enough businesses have opted in, each score is ranked against the peer median for the 28-day reporting period and against the top decile as the peer group grows.

- Peer groups by company size and industry — Choose a company size (e.g., 1–999, 1,000–4,999, or 5,000+ employees) and one of ten industries, then switch between your industry and all industries. If your industry’s peer group is too small, the comparison widens to all industries for your company size, and the dashboard labels the peer group it used.

- Copilot metrics industry comparison policy — Opt in from the dashboard or centrally from your enterprise or organization Copilot policies. Both places use the same policy, so turning it off in either place stops both contributing data and seeing comparisons.

Why this matters

Enterprise leaders can measure their own Copilot adoption, but until now they couldn’t tell whether it was leading or lagging comparable businesses. Industry comparisons add the peer context needed to set realistic goals, identify adoption gaps, and communicate progress.

Important notes

- Rankings appear only after enough businesses have opted in to form a peer group. Especially soon after launch, you might see only the median, a broader peer group than you selected, or no ranking until more peers join. Rankings also aren’t shown when your own score can’t be calculated such as when all your users are already agent-first or multi-agent, leaving no nonagentic baseline for leverage.

- Comparisons refresh daily. When you opt out, comparisons stop appearing right away and your data is excluded starting with the next daily update. Aggregated benchmarks contain no identifying data and are deleted after 30 days.

- On GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, you’re compared only with participants in the same region. Data is never combined across regions.

- Organizations owned by an enterprise participate through their enterprise, and enterprises used only to assign Copilot Business licenses can’t participate. Enterprise owners, and owners of organizations that aren’t owned by an enterprise, can opt in and set the peer group. Anyone who can view the Copilot impact dashboard can see the results. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.

- Industry comparisons appear only in the dashboard. They aren’t included in the Copilot usage metrics API, NDJSON exports, or downloads.

Visit the Copilot impact dashboard documentation to get started.

items.title: Pull requests: Saved whitespace preferences and improved split view
items.lede: Two improvements make it easier to review pull requests in the “Files changed” page:
items.text:
Two improvements make it easier to review pull requests in the “Files changed” page:

- You can save your whitespace visibility preference across pull requests

- New and deleted files now use the full width in split view

Save your whitespace visibility preference

Open Settings → Whitespace changes and choose Always show, Always hide, or Hide for this diff only. Your saved preference is personal and applies across pull requests.

When whitespace is hidden, an active Hide whitespace filter appears beside All commits. Select its X to temporarily show whitespace without changing your saved preference. File counts and diff statistics reflect the displayed diff.

Review new and deleted files in split view

In split view, new and deleted files now span both columns, as they do in unified view. This gives you more room to review new files and reduces line wrapping.

Leave your questions or feedback in our Community discussion.

items.title: Public monitoring now available with data residency
items.lede: Public monitoring is now available in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency (GHEC DR).
items.text:
Public monitoring is now available in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency (GHEC DR).

Public monitoring with data residency

Public monitoring extends secret scanning beyond internal repositories by monitoring public commits across github.com, attributing exposed credentials back to your enterprise in real time.

For enterprises hosted in data residency regions, attribution is powered exclusively by verified domain matching. Because data residency environments maintain strict tenant isolation from github.com, enterprise membership rosters are not shared across the boundary. Instead, when a commit author’s email matches a domain your enterprise has verified, the alert is encrypted and delivered directly to your enterprise dashboard while ensuring data stays within your designated geography.

Eligibility and billing

Public monitoring is available in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers with data residency. Using public monitoring requires an active GitHub Advanced Security or GitHub Secret Protection license. Enterprise admins and enterprise security managers can enable the feature under enterprise security settings.

Public monitoring is included with your GitHub Advanced Security or GitHub Secret Protection license at no additional cost.

Learn more

Learn more about secret scanning and verifying domains for your enterprise, or share your feedback in the community discussion.

items.title: Global default for Copilot features generally available
items.lede: In September, we announced a global default policy for generally available GitHub Copilot features and supported client capabilities on Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise plans.
items.text:
In September, we announced a global default policy for generally available GitHub Copilot features and supported client capabilities on Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise plans. Starting today, we’re gradually rolling out enforcement of the policy through October 26, so it may take effect at different times for different enterprises and organizations. Eligible features left unconfigured will be set according to the global policy. Administrators can still make explicit choices for individual features at any time.

The policy applies to eligible settings on “Features & clients” and “MCP servers in Copilot”. You can review your setting under AI Controls → Copilot → Default policy for new features. For eligibility and exceptions, see the documentation on default availability.

What’s changing

Once the policy takes effect for your enterprise or organization:

- Eligible generally available features and capabilities left Unconfigured will be set according to the selected global default of Enabled, Disabled, or Let organizations decide. This is a one-time change. Subsequent changes to the default policy won’t change feature policies that are already set.

- Explicit choices are preserved. If you’ve enabled or disabled an individual feature, the rollout won’t change that setting.

- Preview features remain opt-in. If you opted into a preview that later becomes generally available, your choice will be preserved. Otherwise, the default policy will apply when it becomes eligible.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

items.title: Custom skills, agents, and MCP servers in usage metrics API
items.lede: Copilot usage metrics now show the names of the skills, custom agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, slash commands, and plugins that your organization creates, instead of grouping them under other or custom. This builds on the agentic CLI customization metrics released in September.
items.text:
Copilot usage metrics now show the names of the skills, custom agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, slash commands, and plugins that your organization creates, instead of grouping them under other or custom. This builds on the agentic CLI customization metrics released in September.

What’s new

- Named entries: In enterprise and organization reports, including per-user 1-day and 28-day reports, aggregated 1-day reports, and day_totals in aggregated 28-day reports, the totals_by_skill, totals_by_custom_agent, totals_by_mcp, totals_by_slash_cmd, and totals_by_plugin arrays now show the configured name of a customer-defined item instead of other or custom.

- More entries: Each totals_by_* list now includes up to 25 entries per record, up from five, so you can see more of the long tail of customizations your developers use. Any remaining activity is combined into a trailing other entry.

- Unchanged counts: interaction_count and the distinct_*_use_count fields are calculated the same way as before.

Why this matters

The customizations that matter most to an organization are often the ones its own teams build. Administrators can now see which internal skills, custom agents, and MCP servers developers actually use, track adoption after rolling out a new one, and focus enablement where it is needed.

Important notes

- Coverage: Names are reported from Copilot CLI (interactive sessions and prompt mode), the GitHub Copilot app, clients built on the Copilot SDK (e.g., VS Code and JetBrains IDEs), and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) integrations. Prompt mode, the app, and ACP integrations require Copilot CLI 1.0.97 or later. Copilot SDK clients require SDK v1.0.21 or later. IDE integrations that aren’t built on the Copilot SDK don’t report names.

- Configured names: Names are reported as they are configured, trimmed and limited to 128 characters. Names that look like file paths stay grouped under other or custom. Review names before sharing reports outside your organization.

- Accuracy: These metrics come from client telemetry and can undercount activity, for example when clients are outdated or telemetry is blocked. Use them to understand trends and adoption rather than for exact accounting.

- History: Names appear starting with report days processed after this release. Earlier days still show other or custom.

- Access: Reports are available to enterprise owners and billing managers, organization owners, and anyone with a custom organization or enterprise role that grants the “View Copilot Metrics” permission. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.

Visit the Copilot usage metrics API documentation to get started.

items.title: GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio — September update
items.lede: September 2026 brought deeper visibility into your work: explore pull requests without leaving chat, bring the AI model your team trusts, and fix vulnerable packages the moment Visual Studio flags them.
items.text:
September 2026 brought deeper visibility into your work: explore pull requests without leaving chat, bring the AI model your team trusts, and fix vulnerable packages the moment Visual Studio flags them.

Highlights

Here’s what’s new with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio 2026. Check the Insiders channel for the latest:

- Explore pull requests with the Git agent: The Git agent can now explore a pull request for you. Open GitHub Copilot Chat, select the Git agent, and attach a pull request as context from the Git Repository window to get a summary with navigable links to the underlying comments and files. This functionality requires connecting your Git provider’s MCP servers; GitHub and Azure DevOps are both supported.

- Updates to Bring Your Own Model (BYOM): BYOM is available in preview and lets you use the models your team prefers, through GitHub Copilot or your own model deployments, whether or not you’re signed in to GitHub. This feature is on by default across the Community, Professional, and Enterprise editions. Breaking change: BYOM now requires the new Agent (Preview), built on the GitHub Copilot SDK-powered harness. The previous Ask and Agent modes no longer support BYOM, and you’ll need to re-add previously configured Ollama models after updating. Supported providers include Microsoft Foundry, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama.

- Fix NuGet Vulnerabilities from the Error List: NuGet Audit warnings in the Error List now include a fixer action that opens GitHub Copilot Chat in agent mode and asks Copilot to fix the vulnerable packages using the NuGet MCP server. This functionality requires signing in to GitHub Copilot and enabling the NuGet MCP server from the Copilot Chat tools menu.

This update is available to users on all GitHub Copilot plans, including Copilot Free, Student, Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise.

Download Visual Studio 2026 to experience all the new Copilot features today. To learn more about what’s new, check out the Visual Studio blog and release notes.

What’s next for Copilot in Visual Studio

Stay up to date on the latest Copilot features by following the Visual Studio blog, where you’ll find roadmap updates and opportunities to share feedback.

items.title: Enterprise installations for GitHub Apps generally available
items.lede: Installing GitHub Apps on your enterprise is now generally available. You can replace classic PATs with GitHub Apps in more of your enterprise and organization automation with the expanded API support detailed below.
items.text:
Installing GitHub Apps on your enterprise is now generally available. You can replace classic PATs with GitHub Apps in more of your enterprise and organization automation with the expanded API support detailed below. These new and expanded permissions are focused on governance, security, and administrative settings for your enterprise, with two gaps at the organization level also closed.

What’s new for GitHub Apps

- Governance: Manage enterprise-level repository policies and rulesets as well as read delegated bypass requests.

- Security: Configure two-factor authentication requirements, verify domains, manage IP allowlists, and control enterprise access restrictions.

- Administration: Update enterprise profiles and manage both member privileges and repository access settings across the enterprise.

New permissions and API coverage

Choose the permissions your workflow needs in your GitHub App settings.

Access |

Enterprise organization and repository policies |
Read/write |
Read policy fields on EnterpriseOwnerInfo. Update private repository forking, default repository permissions, repository visibility changes, repository creation, repository deletion, issue deletion, collaborator invitations, deploy keys, protected branch updates, dependency insights setting, organization projects setting, and repository projects. |

Enterprise bypass requests |
Read |
Read push-rule and repository-policy bypass requests. |

Enterprise settings |

Read enterprise data through EnterpriseOwnerInfo, including server installations and organization invitations. Update the enterprise profile. Read is required for access to the enterprise organization and repository policies. |

Access IpAllowListEntry and associated mutations to create, update, and delete entries on an enterprise or organization IP allowlist. Also toggle allowlist enforcement, trust of GitHub Apps, and user-level enforcement for Enterprise Managed Users. |

Enterprise repository rulesets |

More coverage with existing permissions

Some APIs and objects had gaps in their support for GitHub Apps. These fixes should unblock more automation scenarios with those permissions.

To get started, choose permissions for your GitHub App for the workflows you want to migrate.

These updates will be available in GHES 3.24. For details on using GraphQL with a GitHub App, see Managing an enterprise account with GraphQL. To learn more about enterprise app installations, see Installing a GitHub App on your enterprise.

items.title: Public monitoring adds triage, validity, API, and webhooks
items.lede: Public monitoring now includes alert management capabilities like automatic validity checks to help you triage and remediate leaked secrets at scale.
items.text:
Public monitoring now includes alert management capabilities like automatic validity checks to help you triage and remediate leaked secrets at scale.

- Alert management with dismissals, timelines, and filtering

- Always-on validity checks for supported secret types

- REST API and webhook support for public monitoring alerts

Alert management

Enterprises with public monitoring can now triage findings directly from the enterprise security dashboard:

- Dismiss and reopen alerts: Close alerts as Dismissed or Fixed, provide an optional comment explaining the decision, or reopen closed alerts if circumstances change.

- Activity timeline: Review an audit trail of all actions and state changes taken on an alert.

- Filter and sort: Filter the alert list by repository, committer, secret type, attribution method (membership or verified domain), and state (i.e., open or closed) to focus on the exposures that matter most.

Closing an alert updates its state for your enterprise. It does not revoke the exposed credential or remove it from the public repository.

Always-on validity checks

Public monitoring now automatically checks token validity on an ongoing basis for supported providers. Alerts display whether a credential is Active, Inactive, or Unknown, allowing security teams to quickly prioritize response for live tokens.

REST API and webhook integration

Bring public monitoring findings into your custom incident response pipelines:

- REST API: Enterprise admins and enterprise security managers can query attributed findings programmatically using GET /enterprises/{enterprise}/secret-scanning/public-monitoring-alerts. This returns alert metadata, secret type, attribution, and exposed locations.

- Enterprise webhooks: Subscribe to the secret_scanning_public_monitoring_alert webhook event at the enterprise level to receive real-time notifications whenever a newly detected leak is attributed to your organization.

Eligibility and billing

Public monitoring remains available in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. Enterprise admins and enterprise security managers can enable the feature and manage alert settings from the enterprise security dashboard.

Public monitoring is included with your GitHub Advanced Security or GitHub Secret Protection license at no additional cost.

Learn more

Learn more about public monitoring and join the discussion in the GitHub Community.

items.title: EMU deletions fix
items.lede: Between June 1 and June 13, 2026, some Enterprise Managed User accounts that were deprovisioned through SCIM were incorrectly deleted instead of being suspended and obfuscated as expected.
items.text:
Between June 1 and June 13, 2026, some Enterprise Managed User accounts that were deprovisioned through SCIM were incorrectly deleted instead of being suspended and obfuscated as expected.

As a result, affected users appeared as ghost users in issues, pull requests, and audit logs, rather than retaining their expected suspended and obfuscated user records within the enterprise.

Who was affected

This affected approximately 12,285 Enterprise Managed User accounts across multiple enterprises.

Most affected accounts had already been suspended and hard-deprovisioned, which means they couldn’t be reprovisioned by design. A smaller group of 76 accounts were active at the time of deletion.

How to tell if you were affected

You were affected if your enterprise audit logs contain a user.delete event for an Enterprise Managed User account during the June 1 to June 13, 2026 window. If you do not see any such events in that window, your enterprise was not impacted.

If you do see these events, no action is required from you. GitHub is restoring the affected accounts.

What caused the issue

On June 1, 2026, GitHub enabled a change that routed deprovisioning requests through a new path. That path didn’t correctly check whether the account was an Enterprise Managed User account, which caused the affected accounts to be deleted instead of following the expected suspend-and-obfuscate flow.

GitHub contained the issue by disabling the affected path on June 13, 2026.

What we’re doing to fix it

We’ve made code changes to prevent this from happening again. We’ve also restored affected user records in October 2026.

The restoration process returned affected accounts to their expected suspended and obfuscated state, preserving traceability and audit history within the enterprise. Enterprise owners don’t need to take any action.

Hard-deprovisioned Enterprise Managed User accounts can’t be reprovisioned by design, so this issue doesn’t affect the reprovisioning workflow.

items.title: Turn notifications into code with GitHub Copilot in Teams
items.lede: The new GitHub app in Teams brings notifications and Copilot together, helping teams turn issues into fixes and ship code faster without leaving the conversation.
items.text:
The new GitHub app in Teams brings notifications and Copilot together, helping teams turn issues into fixes and ship code faster without leaving the conversation.

Get notified in channels, group chats, or private chats, then @mention GitHub to turn updates into action.

Turn an issue notification into a pull request

items.title: Usage metrics API adds usage from tools like OpenCode
items.lede: The Copilot usage metrics API now reports model usage from more of the tools your developers use with Copilot, including tools like OpenCode that weren’t previously captured in your reports.
items.text:
The Copilot usage metrics API now reports model usage from more of the tools your developers use with Copilot, including tools like OpenCode that weren’t previously captured in your reports. A new totals_by_client array is available in the enterprise, organization, enterprise-user, and organization-user 1-day and 28-day reports.

What’s new

Each totals_by_client entry represents one client and includes:

- client: The tool that sent the requests, such as opencode, claude_code, codex, zed, copilot_cli, github_app, cloud_agent, code_review, vscode, or jetbrains. Unrecognized clients are grouped under other.

- request_count: The number of successful model requests from the client.

- session_count: The number of distinct sessions from the client.

- token_usage: Prompt tokens, output tokens, and average tokens per request.

- totals_by_model: The same request and token metrics broken down by model, with a model_selection_mode that shows whether the model was requested directly (user_selected), chosen by auto (auto), or chosen by the product (product_selected). Selection modes that aren’t reported individually yet appear as other, and values that can’t be normalized appear as unknown.

Why this matters

More developers now use Copilot as the model provider behind tools outside the IDE. Because those tools often don’t send editor telemetry, their usage was missing from totals_by_ide and hard to account for. Counting requests on the server closes that gap, so you can see which tools drive Copilot usage, compare request and token volume across them, and base tool support and governance decisions on real usage.

This is different from agent app activity, which counts jobs started by agent apps such as Claude and Codex on GitHub. totals_by_client measures model traffic, meaning requests and tokens, from any tool that uses Copilot.

Important notes

- Scope: Enterprise, organization, enterprise-user, and organization-user reports, in both 1-day and 28-day versions. In the aggregated 28-day reports, totals_by_client appears in each day_totals entry.

- Access: Available to enterprise owners and billing managers, organization owners, and anyone with a custom organization or enterprise role that grants the View Copilot Metrics permission. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.

- Copilot code review and Copilot cloud agent: Requests from these clients report product_selected because the product chooses the model. Copilot code review models are reported as unknown.

- Request counts: request_count counts model calls, not prompts. One prompt can trigger several model calls, so don’t compare this field directly with prompt or interaction counts.

- Client identification: Clients are identified by the integration ID they send with each request. Treat client as a best-effort grouping, not a verified identity.

- Backward compatibility: This change is additive. Existing fields are unchanged, and totals_by_client is an empty array when there is no usage to report.

Visit the Copilot usage metrics API documentation to get started.
