items.title: Prioritize Dependabot alerts with reachability analysis
items.lede: Dependabot alerts can add up faster than a team can work through them. A vulnerable package in your dependency tree doesn’t always mean your code uses the vulnerable part of it, so knowing whether it does gives you more context when deciding where to start.
items.text:
Dependabot alerts can add up faster than a team can work through them. A vulnerable package in your dependency tree doesn’t always mean your code uses the vulnerable part of it, so knowing whether it does gives you more context when deciding where to start.

Reachability analysis for Dependabot, now in public preview for JavaScript and TypeScript, adds that context to your alerts. It looks for call paths from your code to the vulnerable functions in your dependencies and shows the evidence on each alert. Use it alongside severity, EPSS score, production context, and your own knowledge of your application to prioritize and remediate dependency vulnerabilities in the way that works for your team.

How it works

Dependabot runs reachability analysis for you in a managed GitHub Actions workflow, so there’s nothing to install or maintain. For each advisory, the analysis uses curated data that identifies the vulnerable functions in the affected package. CodeQL builds a call graph across your repository and its dependencies, then searches it for a path from your code to each of those functions.

Each open Dependabot alert gets one of these verdicts:

- Reachable: Your code has at least one call path to the vulnerable function.

- Potentially reachable: The analysis couldn’t determine whether your code calls the vulnerable function. Treat these alerts as reachable.

- Unreachable: The analysis completed and found no call path to the vulnerable function. These alerts are lower priority.

- Reachability unavailable: The alert couldn’t be analyzed. Triage it as you normally would.

Verdicts appear on the Dependabot alerts you already use, and they never close or dismiss an alert. Filter and sort by verdict on the repository and organization alerts pages, or use the Dependabot alerts REST API to bring the same signal into your own tools and agents.

Availability and requirements

During the public preview:

- Cost: Free. You don’t need a GitHub Advanced Security license and you aren’t billed for the GitHub Actions minutes the analysis uses.

- Plans: GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

- Languages: JavaScript and TypeScript with an npm, Yarn, or pnpm lockfile in the repository.

- Runners: The analysis runs on GitHub-hosted runners. Self-hosted runners aren’t supported during the preview. As with Dependabot updates, you don’t need to turn on GitHub Actions for the analysis to run.

- Repository size and code complexity: Some monorepos and/or repositories with manifest files in multiple directories may not be supported during the preview. During the preview, if analysis runs for longer than three hours, some results might show “Reachability unavailable”.

- Advisory coverage: All GitHub-reviewed JavaScript advisories from the GitHub Advisory Database that receive Dependabot alerts are covered.

Get started

Reachability analysis is off by default. Turn it on for many repositories at once with a custom security configuration for your enterprise or organization, or for a single repository in the Dependabot section of Settings > Advanced Security. Dependabot alerts must be on to see reachability verdicts.

The first scan starts right away and can take from a few minutes to a few hours. Scans then rerun daily while the repository has open Dependabot alerts, so verdicts keep up as your code and advisories change.

To learn more, see About reachability analysis for Dependabot alerts in GitHub Docs.

If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment in our Community discussion.

items.title: Introducing Replica, an open-source AI prototyping tool
items.lede: We’re open sourcing Replica, an AI-powered prototyping tool created by GitHub Design that helps anyone on your product team turn ideas into interactive prototypes using your own design system.
items.text:
We’re open sourcing Replica, an AI-powered prototyping tool created by GitHub Design that helps anyone on your product team turn ideas into interactive prototypes using your own design system.

Music: “Electrodoodle” by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), licensed under CC BY 4.0. Excerpted, level-adjusted and faded for this video.

Great product ideas can come from anywhere, but turning them into something tangible often takes time and specialized skills. Replica makes it easier for designers, product managers, and engineers to explore ideas together, get feedback earlier, and iterate without starting from scratch.

Unlike generic AI prototyping tools, Replica uses your team’s existing components, patterns, and documentation to guide what gets created. Designers define the guidance, while anyone on the team can use natural language in the GitHub Copilot app to create and refine prototypes that reflect how your product actually works.

What can you do with Replica?

- Prototype with your design system: Use your existing components, patterns, and documentation to guide AI-generated prototypes.

- Turn ideas into interactive experiences: Describe what you want to explore in natural language, then see, test, and refine the result alongside your Copilot conversation.

- Collaborate and gather feedback: Publish prototypes to an optional, self-hosted Replica Hub where teammates can explore them and leave comments.

- Adapt Replica to your team: Customize the open-source tooling and guidance to fit your product and workflows.

Replica helps teams move from conversations to tangible experiences faster, so they can test assumptions, explore possibilities, and make better-informed product decisions together.

Get started

Replica is available now as an open-source project under the MIT license.

You can start prototyping locally or set up Replica Hub to share prototypes with your team. Explore the repository for setup instructions, documentation, and examples.

Explore Replica on GitHub.

We’re excited to share what we’ve been building at GitHub Design and see what the community creates with it. Feedback, ideas, and contributions are welcome!

items.title: GitHub Copilot Fusion now supports selection of local models
items.lede: Today we are shipping intelligent routing for local models into experimental preview. GitHub Copilot Fusion can now choose between supported on-device models and cloud models, enabling intelligent local model routing in GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot app, and Visual Studio Code.
items.text:
Today we are shipping intelligent routing for local models into experimental preview. GitHub Copilot Fusion can now choose between supported on-device models and cloud models, enabling intelligent local model routing in GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot app, and Visual Studio Code. This opt-in experimental preview lets you use your device’s compute without switching models manually for each request. For a deeper dive into this feature, see our original announcement on October 7th.

Managed download and setup on Windows

On supported Windows devices, you can download and configure MAI Code 1.1 Flash through the Windows ML provider.

- In Copilot CLI, enable experimental mode and open /model to follow the setup prompts.

- In the Copilot app, configure the Windows ML provider under Settings > Model providers, enable Local model auto routing under Settings > Experiments, and start a new session. Windows ML local models is enabled by default on Windows.

- In VS Code, enable chat.copilot.localModel.enabled.

Once the model is ready, select Standard in Copilot Fusion to let Copilot choose between local and cloud models. You can also select the local model directly for your session.

Bring your own local model

The managed download experience is Windows-only, but Copilot CLI’s local Copilot Fusion routing also works with manually configured models on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

You can configure MAI Code 1.1 Flash or Qwen3.8 Flash Next through a local OpenAI-compatible server. You manage the model download and inference runtime, and your device must have sufficient resources to run it. Configure the model as a supported local-model provider, enable experimental local routing, and select Standard in Copilot Fusion to let Copilot choose between eligible local and cloud models.

This builds on the recent local-model discovery improvements in Copilot CLI. Adding or discovering a model through bring your own key (BYOK) configuration doesn’t automatically make it eligible for Copilot Fusion.

The Copilot app also supports connecting and directly selecting compatible local models through BYOK. However, its intelligent routing currently supports managed Windows ML models only.

Local inference doesn’t make your session offline. Copilot Fusion still makes routing decisions in the cloud, and local models may have different safety protections from Copilot-provided cloud models.

For setup instructions, see Adding LLM models to GitHub Copilot CLI and Adding LLM models to the GitHub Copilot app. For routing behavior, see our docs on intelligent routing to local models.

items.title: GitHub Copilot in JetBrains Universe releases
items.lede: Today, we’re making GitHub Copilot in JetBrains more capable, secure, and seamless. From GitHub Copilot Fusion’s smarter model orchestration to local sandboxes and next edit suggestions (NES), this update brings powerful improvements to how you build, review, and manage work.
items.text:
Today, we’re making GitHub Copilot in JetBrains more capable, secure, and seamless. From GitHub Copilot Fusion’s smarter model orchestration to local sandboxes and next edit suggestions (NES), this update brings powerful improvements to how you build, review, and manage work.

What’s new

GitHub Copilot Fusion

GitHub Copilot Fusion is now available for Copilot users in JetBrains IDEs. Copilot Fusion delivers stronger task-completion results at lower cost without requiring users to choose and coordinate models themselves. Select Standard, High, or Max based on the level of effort a task requires, and Copilot determines whether to use a single model or combine multiple models while balancing quality, speed, and cost.

Copilot Fusion replaces the current Auto model option and is gradually rolling out to all GitHub Copilot users. Copilot Fusion use is discounted 30% for the first 30 days.

Local sandboxes are now generally available

Local sandboxing for GitHub Copilot in JetBrains is now generally available. Local sandboxes give developers a secure execution boundary for agentic workflows on their own machines. Tools and commands initiated by Copilot run with restricted access to the filesystem, network, credentials, and other system capabilities, based on policies defined by the developer or their organization.

Next edit suggestions (NES) generally available

Next edit suggestions (NES) are now generally available in JetBrains IDEs, with higher suggestion quality, better context awareness, and a smoother experience for reviewing and applying suggestions inline as you work.

Agent harness

The Microsoft Copilot agent harness is now the default harness for all users when available.

Session sidebar

Use the session sidebar button to open sessions side by side directly from individual sessions.

Default session permissions

You can now configure the default permission mode for new Copilot sessions in settings. Choose a default so you don’t need to select the same permission mode each time you start a session.

User experience enhancements

- Settings access: Find GitHub Copilot at the top level of IDE settings.

- Agent selection: Find Copilot ahead of Local in the agent picker when both providers are enabled.

- Completion flow: Get better coordination between inline completions and next edit suggestions, including follow-up suggestions after accepting a completion.

- Account notifications: See concise, timed messages for sign-in, sign-out, and account switches, including the authenticated account name after a successful switch when it’s available.

- Plugin updates: Open the Plugins Marketplace filtered to the official GitHub Copilot plugin directly from Copilot update prompts.

- Turn details: Hover over a Copilot agent turn to see completion time, generation time, and per-model token usage.

Quality improvements

This update improves edit reliability, cancellation recovery, and selected-code context so you can work with fewer interruptions or lost changes. It also addresses problems with customization access on Windows and WSL, prompt templates after language server restarts, and IDE responsiveness.

Try it out

Try the latest version of the GitHub Copilot plugin and share your feedback to help us improve it.

Share your feedback

Share your experience through these channels:

- In-product feedback: Use the feedback options within your IDE.

- Feedback repository: Share your thoughts in the GitHub Copilot for JetBrains IDEs issues.

links.text: latest version of the GitHub Copilot plugin
GitHub Copilot for JetBrains IDEs issues

items.title: Generate and edit images directly in Copilot
items.lede: You can now generate and edit images using natural language in GitHub Copilot. When you ask for an image, your selected reasoning model calls a dedicated image-generation tool powered by GPT Image 2.5 Flare, previews the result inline, and saves it to your project.
items.text:
You can now generate and edit images using natural language in GitHub Copilot. When you ask for an image, your selected reasoning model calls a dedicated image-generation tool powered by GPT Image 2.5 Flare, previews the result inline, and saves it to your project.

Previously, getting a visual asset while working in Copilot meant stepping away to a separate tool, describing what you needed again, generating it there, and manually bringing it back into your project. This update removes that context switch, so you can go from an idea to a usable image without breaking your flow.

- Describe an image conversationally in any Copilot chat session, whether you’re starting a new request or in the middle of a coding task.

- Copilot previews the generated image inline and saves it directly to your workspace.

- Organization and enterprise owners can turn off image generation by disabling the image generation model using Copilot model policies.

- You can opt in to a visible “Made with AI” watermark on images Copilot generates and edits. Watermarking is off by default.

To try it, open a Copilot chat in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, or Copilot CLI and describe the image you want.

Image generation is in public preview for Copilot Pro, Copilot Pro+, Copilot Business, and Copilot Enterprise. It’s billed separately from your chat model, based on image tokens that count toward your plan’s AI credits.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

items.title: GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available
items.lede: GitHub Agentic Workflows, an open source project from GitHub Next, is now generally available. With agentic workflows, you can automate reasoning-based tasks like issue triage, CI failure analysis, documentation updates, and test writing by using coding agents inside GitHub Actions.
items.text:
GitHub Agentic Workflows, an open source project from GitHub Next, is now generally available. With agentic workflows, you can automate reasoning-based tasks like issue triage, CI failure analysis, documentation updates, and test writing by using coding agents inside GitHub Actions.

Define your automation in natural language Markdown files, and GitHub Agentic Workflows compiles them into standard Actions YAML. Because these are GitHub Actions, they reuse your existing runner groups and policy constraints. You can use GitHub Copilot or bring your own coding agent to power each workflow.

We’ve been rolling out our agentic developer workflows, and the results are measurable. One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone. Across his team, measured velocity has more than doubled on average, and AI now authors 91% of the team’s commits. With these workflows, the team cut production errors from about 11,000 a day to under 1,000 and drove a technology migration end to end.

One workflow takes a feature from requirements to implementation with validation evidence. Others keep our frameworks current and steadily raise code quality and test coverage. Because AI drives the process to completion, our engineers can run four or five efforts in parallel and stay focused on the bigger goals.

Ben Alton – Senior manager, Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team at Accenture

Built-in safeguards

GitHub Agentic Workflows incorporates layered safeguards for your automation. Agents access GitHub content respecting the integrity filter rules, run with read-only permissions by default, and execute inside a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall. The outputs are validated through the safe outputs process, and a dedicated threat detection job scans all proposed changes before they are applied.

Additional capabilities for general availability

Highlights since the public preview include:

- Actions Runner Controller (ARC) and Docker-in-Docker support: Run agentic workflows on self-hosted ARC runners with Docker-in-Docker.

- Improved budget forecasting: gh aw forecast is no longer experimental. It now includes both threat detection credits and monthly ranges for a fuller picture of your AI credit spend.

- New models, engine choices, and workflows: The model inventory has been refreshed, model providers can be picked per workflow, and there are new workflow templates that can be added with gh aw add-wizard.

- Model routing: Workflows can use a model router that optimizes for task type and difficulty.

- Improved agent isolation: Agents can run in a Cloud Hypervisor or NVX micro-VM and prevent data leaks in cross-repository workflows with enclaves.

See the GitHub Agentic Workflows release notes for the full list of changes.

Get started

Follow the quickstart guide to install the CLI extension and trigger your first workflow in minutes. Explore prebuilt workflows in GitHub Next’s agentics repository for ready-to-use examples covering triage, dependency management, code review, and reporting.

GitHub Agentic Workflows is now generally available on github.com for GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise. Using the default GitHub Copilot CLI engine to power a workflow requires a Copilot license.

Learn more in the GitHub Agentic Workflows documentation, and join the conversation in the community discussion.

items.title: Work from anywhere with a new, connected Copilot cloud experience
items.lede: Copilot is now one connected experience in the cloud. Start a cloud task wherever you are, on github.com, GitHub Mobile, the Copilot CLI, the Copilot app, VS Code, or right from a conversation in Slack or Microsoft Teams. Then pick it up wherever you work next.
items.text:
Copilot is now one connected experience in the cloud. Start a cloud task wherever you are, on github.com, GitHub Mobile, the Copilot CLI, the Copilot app, VS Code, or right from a conversation in Slack or Microsoft Teams. Then pick it up wherever you work next.

By default, every session runs in a secure cloud sandbox that starts fast and resumes right where you left off. The compute behind it can now be drawn from your included Actions entitlement, the same one that already runs your builds. That entitlement is now one flexible pool you can use for builds, cloud sandboxes, and, on Team and Enterprise Cloud, larger hosted runners.

The new Copilot cloud experience across surfaces (e.g., Web, Mobile, App, CLI, VS Code, Slack, and Microsoft Teams) and cloud sandboxes are both generally available on paid Copilot plans.

Why this new connected experience matters

- One session, every surface. Start a change on your phone with voice or a screenshot, continue it on the web, and finish it in the Copilot app, VS Code, or CLI. It’s the same session the whole way, and every surface shows the same session list.

- Secure ephemeral isolated environments for agents that start fast and resume where you left off. By default, every session runs in a cloud sandbox, which is a secure environment on GitHub-managed infrastructure, separate from your local machine. Sandboxes start fast and have no one-hour limit on total running session time. When a sandbox shuts down, it saves a snapshot, so you can resume the session later from any surface. Cloud sandboxes let you run agents without being limited by your local machine’s compute resources.

- Flexible compute entitlement. Your included Actions compute entitlement is now one shared, dollar-based pool instead of a fixed number of standard runner minutes. It covers standard GitHub-hosted runners, cloud sandboxes, and, on Team and Enterprise Cloud, larger hosted runners. You can choose the compute that best fits each task, and each product keeps its own published rate.

Start cloud sessions and continue your work anywhere

On github.com and GitHub Mobile, you can chat and kick off code changes in the same conversation, with the same deep integration with your GitHub workflow as Copilot Chat and Copilot coding agent. Ask a question across multiple repositories in an organization or pick a repository for a code change. In Slack or Teams, mention @GitHub to create an issue, request a code change, or investigate a bug.

- Start from anywhere: Kick off a cloud session from github.com, the Copilot CLI, the Copilot app, VS Code, or the redesigned Copilot experience on GitHub Mobile. On mobile, start a new session from the Copilot tab, or select New agent session from any pull request, issue, or repository to get started right where you’re working.

- Describe the task your way: On GitHub Mobile, describe a task by voice or attach an image or file. On the web, attach repositories, Copilot Spaces, or files with the (+) menu or @. In Slack and Teams, Copilot can use messages and threads as context.

- Unified context across surfaces: On github.com, when you open Copilot over a pull request, file, or repository, it adds that page as context. Your sessions follow you, and pins sync across the web and mobile.

- Steer local sessions from your phone: Register your local device through GitHub Mission Control as an environment in the Copilot CLI or VS Code, then start and steer your sessions on the go with GitHub Mobile (iOS, Android).

For more information, see the documentation on using Copilot in a cloud environment.

Give Copilot the tools & context it needs

Cloud sessions have the same tools as the Copilot CLI and Copilot app, plus ways to bring in context and customize how Copilot works:

- Tools: Bash and the GitHub CLI work alongside code search for everyday tasks, such as tracing a bug to a specific pull request or bulk-moving issues between epics.

- Connectors and MCP: Built-in connectors bring in context from Sentry, Linear, Cloudflare, and more. Set them up once in the Customize menu on GitHub or in the Copilot app, and they work in every cloud session.

items.title: GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Universe releases
items.lede: This year, we focused on giving you more choice in how you work with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code: which models you use, where your agents run, and how you stay involved.
items.text:
This year, we focused on giving you more choice in how you work with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code: which models you use, where your agents run, and how you stay involved.

Keep work moving without staying at your desk or in one tool. With GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code, start a cloud agent session from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check on it from github.com at lunch. Session continuity lets you pick up the same session across these clients while your agent keeps working in the cloud.

Start and follow cloud sessions across Copilot clients

Hand off work without keeping your computer on. Start a cloud agent session from the Agents window in VS Code. The work runs on GitHub’s infrastructure, so closing your laptop doesn’t stop it.

Find and continue the same session in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, GitHub Mobile, github.com, or Copilot CLI. Sessions started in a Slack or Microsoft Teams DM can also be continued in these clients.

Keep agents working on your own machines

Move on to another task or project without worrying about losing your session. The new Agent Host isolates your Copilot sessions from individual VS Code windows, so work continues in the background after you close the project folder or window.

You can also run agents on a separate machine while you use your primary development machine for other work. The power and flexibility of VS Code’s Remote SSH and dev tunnels extends to the Agents window. The remote agent works with the same code, tools, and dependencies, and can keep running when you disconnect or quit VS Code locally. The remote machine and its Agent Host must remain running.

Move between the editor and Agents windows

Switch between the editor and the Agents window without starting over. Both views stay in sync with the same live Copilot session.

Control agents on your machine from your phone

Check progress, give direction, or start a new task on your development machine from GitHub Mobile. Your phone provides the controls, and the agent does the work on your development machine. To get started, open a terminal on that machine and run the VS Code CLI command code agent host --github-environment from your project folder. Keep the machine and its Agent Host running while you use it from your phone.

Get a more consistent GitHub Copilot

Get more consistent agent behavior across VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. The Copilot harness, built on the Microsoft Copilot SDK, is now the default for new sessions in both the editor and the Agents window.

Install GitHub Copilot CLI with VS Code

Bring Copilot to your terminal with less setup. Install GitHub Copilot CLI through the VS Code installer on Windows, when adding VS Code to your path on macOS, or by running copilot on Linux.

Compare model results

Explore different approaches to the same coding task. Run models and harnesses in parallel in the Agents window, then review their results side by side. You can ask a Judge model to recommend a solution and choose Synthesize to combine ideas from the other attempts. This is in preview.

Let your agent use your desktop apps

Give your agent tasks that need more than code or terminal commands. With computer use, Copilot can read and interact with desktop apps, including clicking controls and editing text.

On macOS or Windows, open VS Code Settings, search for chat.agentHost.computerUse.enabled, and enable it. Restart VS Code, then run /computer on in a Copilot session running on your computer.

Each application requires your approval. Computer use shares its setup with Copilot CLI and the GitHub Copilot app, so on macOS you grant the required system permissions once. Organizations can disable computer use through policy.

This is an experimental feature.

Build your own client

Bring session continuity to your own app. Build a client that connects to an Agent Host and works with the same live sessions as VS Code.

The open Agent Host Protocol (AHP) lets connected clients stay in sync and catch up after reconnecting. Run code agent host, then connect with a client library for TypeScript, Rust, Go, Kotlin, or Swift.

items.title: Route and orchestrate models with GitHub Copilot Fusion
items.lede: GitHub Copilot Fusion is generally available. Instead of picking a model for each task, choose Copilot Fusion and let Copilot intelligently route and orchestrate which models it uses for you.
items.text:
GitHub Copilot Fusion is generally available. Instead of picking a model for each task, choose Copilot Fusion and let Copilot intelligently route and orchestrate which models it uses for you.

Copilot Fusion brings together Project HydraFusion’s multi-model orchestration and Copilot auto model selection’s fine-tuned model selection, leveraging the benefits of both to balance performance and cost efficiency.

Since Project HydraFusion launched, we’ve improved its performance. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Copilot Fusion Max scored 60, within two points of Claude Code with Opus 5.5 Max. It delivered that result at about half the average API cost per task, using about half as many tokens and taking about 40% less time per task.

Smarter choices for developers

When you select Copilot Fusion in the model picker, you aren’t selecting a specific model. You’re choosing a system that routes and orchestrates models for each task. There’s no need to switch models during a task or decide which model suits each step. For each prompt, Copilot Fusion determines which models to use and how they work together, while you choose the right level of effort.

To use it, select Copilot Fusion in the model picker, then choose the effort level.

- Fusion Standard: Prioritizes versatile models for everyday coding.

- Fusion High: Prioritizes capable models for challenging tasks and deeper reasoning.

- Fusion Max: Prioritizes the most capable models for the most demanding tasks and complex reasoning.

Watch as Copilot Fusion analyzes each task and selects a model to complete it, orchestrating multiple models through the following workflows when needed.

- Single: One model solves the task directly.

- Cascade: An efficient model drafts a response. A quality check determines whether to accept it or escalate to a stronger model.

- Critique: One model drafts an initial response, another model reviews it, and the original model revises.

More control for administrators

Administrators control which models Copilot Fusion can use and whether Copilot Fusion is the default.

- Copilot Fusion only uses the models that are enabled in your enterprise and organization model policies. Enterprise administrators can view what models Copilot Fusion picks from, independently set each model’s effective policy state, and disable models for Copilot Fusion without disabling the model for everyone. See Manage availability of default models.

- Administrators can set Copilot Fusion, at any effort level, as the default model for Copilot users with Enterprise managed settings. To configure settings, see Enterprise managed settings.

“GitHub Copilot Fusion Standard has improved token efficiency across AT&T by automatically selecting the right model for the task, reducing unnecessary spend and preserving capacity for higher-value work. Previously, developers would often choose a more powerful model for a complex task and forget to switch back for everyday activities. Copilot Fusion eliminates that friction, optimizing model selection without requiring developers to manage it themselves. We’ve also seen its decision-making improve over time, giving developers greater confidence to focus on their work while Copilot handles model selection.”

Hari Pokhrel, Principal Software Engineer, AT&T

Billing

When you use Copilot Fusion you’re billed for each model it uses, at each model’s standard rate. For a limited time, users on paid Copilot plans will receive a 30% discount on model costs when using Copilot Fusion.

Get started

Copilot Fusion is available on all Copilot plans in Visual Studio Code, the GitHub Copilot app, GitHub Copilot CLI, and JetBrains IDEs. Support for additional clients is coming soon.

Update your client to try it out. Open the model picker, select Copilot Fusion, and choose an effort level.

Note for research preview participants: if you previously enabled auto, HydraFusion, or HydraFusion Max, your selections will automatically transition to the corresponding Copilot Fusion effort levels.

To learn more, see our documentation on GitHub Copilot Fusion and share your feedback in the GitHub Community.

items.title: Security extension for the GitHub Copilot app
items.lede: You can now work through your repository’s GitHub code scanning alerts without leaving the GitHub Copilot app. The new GitHub security extension, now in public preview, lets you find the alerts that matter most and ask Copilot to explain or help fix them.
items.text:
You can now work through your repository’s GitHub code scanning alerts without leaving the GitHub Copilot app. The new GitHub security extension, now in public preview, lets you find the alerts that matter most and ask Copilot to explain or help fix them.

Until now, fixing a code scanning alert meant switching between the alert on github.com and the code in your editor. With the security extension, you can move from finding an alert to fixing it in one place.

Fix the alerts already in your code

If you already run code scanning on your repository, the security extension shows its open code scanning alerts:

- Browse every open code scanning alert, ordered by severity, and use search and filters to narrow the list.

- Open an alert to see its details and the affected code. You can open the full alert page on github.com when you need more context.

- Select one or more alerts and ask Copilot to Explain or Fix them. Copilot only makes fixes in your local working copy and doesn’t commit or push anything. This way you can review and iterate on the changes in the app and push when you’re ready.

- See linked pull requests on an alert so you know whether someone is already working on a fix.

- Dismiss alerts you don’t plan to fix. If your organization uses delegated alert dismissal, the extension sends your dismissal for approval.

Catch new issues before you open a pull request

- Run /security-review on your current changes and see those findings next to your existing alerts.

- The extension tells you when your code has changed since the last review so you know when to run it again.

You can also ask Copilot about your alerts in chat. Copilot uses the security extension’s tools in the same way as any other tool, following your tool permission settings.

Get started

To install the security extension:

- In your terminal run copilot plugin install github-security@awesome-copilot.

- In the GitHub Copilot app, click Customize, search for github-security, then click + Install.

The extension is automatically enabled, and you can open the Security canvas from a session for your repository.

The Explain, Fix, and /security-review actions use the model you’ve selected in the app and consume AI credits in the same way as any other prompt. Browsing and dismissing alerts don’t use AI.

The security extension is in public preview on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. GitHub Enterprise Server isn’t supported.

- With any Copilot plan: You can install the extension and run /security-review on your local changes. For Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise, an administrator needs to enable the GitHub Copilot app policy, and can use enterprise managed settings to control which plugins developers can install.

- With code scanning: You can see, fix, and dismiss existing alerts for repositories where code scanning is enabled and you have permission to view the alerts. Private repositories need GitHub Code Security for this.

Learn more in the security extension documentation and join the discussion in GitHub Community.

items.title: AI Scan for repositories in public preview
items.lede: You can now use AI Scan to find vulnerabilities across your whole repository, not just in pull request changes. It covers languages and frameworks that CodeQL doesn’t support and finds issues that rule-based analysis can miss in languages CodeQL already covers.
items.text:
You can now use AI Scan to find vulnerabilities across your whole repository, not just in pull request changes. It covers languages and frameworks that CodeQL doesn’t support and finds issues that rule-based analysis can miss in languages CodeQL already covers. Findings appear in your GitHub code scanning alert list alongside CodeQL alerts.

How it works

- Once your enterprise has enabled the AI Scan policy, organization owners and security managers can turn on AI Scan for repositories for their organization. For repositories owned by personal accounts, you turn it on in repository settings. This setting is separate from AI Scan for pull requests.

- After AI Scan for repositories is enabled, users with write access to code scanning can start a scan from the Code scanning page. Each scan analyzes the latest commit on the default branch.

- An agentic code scanner explores your repository and focuses on the code most likely to contain vulnerabilities. Each scan runs within a fixed time budget, which keeps its cost bounded.

- When both AI Scan and CodeQL are scanning the same repository, AI Scan skips issues that CodeQL already reports.

- On rescans, AI Scan keeps existing findings open if it detects them again and only reports new findings.

Working with AI Scan alerts

AI Scan alerts flow into the code scanning backlog just like other code scanning alerts and support the same workflows, such as assignees, linked pull requests, and issues. You can fix them with agentic autofix or add them to security campaigns. AI Scan alerts don’t automatically close when you merge a fix. Start a new scan after merging to check and close any alerts you’ve fixed.

Availability

AI Scan for repositories is available on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. A GitHub Copilot license isn’t required.

- Organization-owned repositories: Available for public repositories as well as for both private and internal repositories with GitHub Code Security or GitHub Advanced Security.

- Repositories owned by personal accounts: Available for public repositories. Private repositories owned by personal accounts aren’t supported.

Billing

AI Scan for repositories consumes Code Security AI credits. Usage appears in the “AI usage” section of enterprise billing and licensing under the “Advanced Security” product. You can set SKU-level budgets for Code Security AI credits, and if you’ve used up your budget, GitHub tells you before a scan starts. For public repositories owned by a personal account, usage is billed to that personal account, unless the repository owner has a GitHub Copilot license provided by an organization or enterprise. In that case, usage is billed to that organization or enterprise. Learn more about billing for GitHub Advanced Security AI features.

Learn more about AI Scan and join the discussion in GitHub Community.

items.title: Code scanning for AI applications in public preview
items.lede: Code scanning can now detect AI applications and agent vulnerabilities, including indirect prompt injection (XPIA), sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency, and other AI-specific risks as coverage expands. Scans automatically run on pull requests.
items.text:
Code scanning can now detect AI applications and agent vulnerabilities, including indirect prompt injection (XPIA), sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency, and other AI-specific risks as coverage expands. Scans automatically run on pull requests.

Here’s an overview of AI applications and agent vulnerabilities that are covered:

- Indirect prompt injection is the top risk in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. It happens when malicious instructions are hidden in untrusted content (e.g., a file, webpage, or issue comment) that an AI agent reads. If that agent also has access to tools, data, or business systems, those hidden instructions can manipulate its behavior or trigger unintended actions. As more teams build agents into their codebases, these risky architectures can be difficult to spot through manual review alone.

- Sensitive information disclosure happens when an AI application or agent can access sensitive data without appropriate authorization controls, potentially exposing it to users or systems that should not have access.

- Excessive agency happens when an AI agent has more capabilities, permissions, or autonomy than its task requires, increasing the risk of unintended or high-impact actions.

Code scanning for AI applications:

- Scans pull requests automatically when they’re created, alongside your existing CodeQL analysis.

- Flags agent code paths where untrusted content can reach a model that has access to tools, data, or business systems.

- Provides actionable mitigation guidance directly in the pull request so you can address the risk before it ships.

If your organization uses GitHub Advanced Security, this detector starts scanning pull requests in repositories where code scanning and scans for AI applications are enabled. Review any new alerts on the Conversation or Files changed tab of your pull requests, and use the provided guidance to remediate before merging.

Code scanning for AI applications is now in public preview on github.com and requires a GitHub Advanced Security license. It isn’t available on GitHub Enterprise Server at this time.

Learn more about AI applications code scanning on pull requests and join the discussion in GitHub Community.

items.title: Push protection beyond predefined secret patterns
items.lede: GitHub push protection is expanding beyond secrets with predefined formats.
items.text:
GitHub push protection is expanding beyond secrets with predefined formats.

Developed in collaboration with Microsoft Applied Sciences, our new purpose-built classifier evaluates how potential secrets are used in surrounding code, allowing GitHub to block secrets even without a known and recognizable format.

What’s new

Starting today, you can enable push protection for AI-detected secrets for repositories with both push protection and AI-detected secret scans already enabled. The feature is available in public preview.

Until now, push protection relied on predefined patterns to recognize secret types. Our new classifier introduces context-aware detection directly into the push path, allowing developers to catch and block more secrets before they enter repository history. Once enabled, it runs alongside pattern-based detectors, extending their coverage for new pushes, commits in the GitHub UI, and file uploads. If it detects a secret, GitHub rejects the change and reports the location of the secret.

In early results, the classifier more than doubled the number of pushes where push protection caught a secret, with a user-reported precision rate rivaling that of issuer-defined detectors from our secret scanning partners.

To resolve a block, remove the secret from every commit in the push and try again. Existing bypass and delegated bypass workflows still apply. Agents must get authorization before bypassing or working around a block.

Availability and enablement

The classifier is off by default in push protection. The feature can be enabled for repositories, organizations, enterprises, and enterprise-managed users.

To enable the feature, a repository must have both AI-detected secrets and push protection already enabled.

Repository admins can enable the feature from their repository settings page: Settings > Advanced Security > Secret Protection > AI-detected secrets > Block AI-detected secrets.

Organization and enterprise admins can enable the feature from security configurations: Settings > Advanced Security > Security Configurations > Secret Protection > Secret scanning > AI-detected secrets > Block AI-detected secrets. Create or edit a custom security configuration with GitHub Secret Protection (GHSP) or GitHub Advanced Security (GHAS) and secret scanning enabled. Set each of the following settings to Enabled in the UI, or enabled through the security configurations REST API:

UI setting |
REST API field |

AI-detected secrets |
secret_scanning_generic_secrets |

Push protection |
secret_scanning_push_protection |

Block AI-detected secrets |
secret_scanning_generic_secrets_push_protection |

Apply the configuration to the repositories you want to protect.

The preview is available to organizations with GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Advanced Security on github.com. AI detection in push protection consumes AI credits. Billing begins once you opt in to the public preview and enable the feature. AI-detected secret alerts from post-push scanning remain included with GHSP and GHAS at no additional charge.

Learn more about secret scanning and push protection in our product documentation.

items.title: Public monitoring for enterprises generally available
items.lede: GitHub public monitoring alerts enterprises when their secrets are publicly exposed anywhere on GitHub, helping teams respond quickly to leaks wherever they happen. It’s now generally available to enterprises with GitHub Secret Protection at no additional cost.
items.text:
GitHub public monitoring alerts enterprises when their secrets are publicly exposed anywhere on GitHub, helping teams respond quickly to leaks wherever they happen. It’s now generally available to enterprises with GitHub Secret Protection at no additional cost.

What is public monitoring?

GitHub monitors the entire public surface of github.com for leaked secrets in real time. Public monitoring attributes those secrets back to your enterprise, based on where your people commit.

Secret scanning has always protected the repositories you own, but secrets leak beyond that boundary. For example, a developer commits to a personal fork or an open source project or they paste a token into a public issue or pull request. This often happens from an account your security team isn’t tracking. Exposures like these were nearly impossible to find and often only surfaced after they’d been abused by bad actors.

Public monitoring closes that gap. It finds these vulnerabilities and attributes them to your enterprise so you can respond quickly. The feature scans for secrets exposed anywhere in public content across github.com (e.g., git content, pull request comments, and user-created gists) and natively attributes each one back to your enterprise through GitHub’s identity layer and verified domains.

Because the activity happens on GitHub, so does the attribution: in real time (not a nightly async crawl), definitively with native platform metadata (not on a guess from a commit email), and across arbitrary public repositories (not just surfaces where you tell us to look).

Public monitoring will never scan private repositories; it surfaces only secrets that are already exposed publicly, so you can revoke leaked secrets before they’re abused by bad actors. Secret scanning for enterprises remains available for scanning all repositories owned by your organization or enterprise, including public, private, or internal repositories.

Public monitoring works out of the box with no setup or configuration required. Just enable it and start seeing results.

Why are we doing this?

GitHub is committed to empowering the developer community by helping organizations recognize and address the risks of secret leaks wherever they happen. We believe every enterprise should know the moment its secrets leak in public, no matter where it happens on GitHub. That’s why public monitoring is now generally available for enterprises with GitHub Secret Protection, at no additional cost.

Secrets don’t respect boundaries; scanning for them shouldn’t either.

How does attribution work?

GitHub attributes a public finding to your enterprise using two main heuristics: verified domain matching and enterprise membership. Both leverage metadata across GitHub’s identity layer, including emails verified for a user’s account, to match findings to an enterprise.

Method |
What it checks |
Catches |

Member-based attribution |
The committer’s GitHub account belongs to your enterprise as an enterprise member |
Leaks from managed accounts and known members |

Verified domain matching |
The committer’s email is on a domain your organization or enterprise has verified |
Leaks from personal accounts using a work email |

Verified domain matching applies even when the account isn’t linked to your enterprise and even when the email isn’t public. Each finding shows which method attributed it, along with the secret type, the public location (e.g. file, issue, pull request, discussion, etc.), and the committer.

Is public monitoring with data residency available?

Yes, public monitoring is supported for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers with data residency.

For enterprises hosted in data residency regions, attribution is powered exclusively by verified domain matching. Because data residency environments maintain strict tenant isolation from github.com, enterprise membership rosters are not shared across the boundary. Instead, when a commit author’s email matches a domain your enterprise has verified, the alert is encrypted and delivered directly to your enterprise dashboard while ensuring data stays within your designated geography.

items.title: Issue artifacts are now in public preview
items.lede: Issue artifacts attach agent-generated outputs and other important context directly to an issue. By keeping plans, research, links, and visualizations alongside the work, they give coding agents richer context and teams a durable record as the work evolves.
items.text:
Issue artifacts attach agent-generated outputs and other important context directly to an issue. By keeping plans, research, links, and visualizations alongside the work, they give coding agents richer context and teams a durable record as the work evolves.

With issue artifacts, you can attach:

- Markdown files for plans, research, root cause analyses, and other documents.

- Links to Slack or Microsoft Teams threads, prototypes, and other external resources.

- HTML files for interactive visualizations, flowcharts, and diagrams, with the ability to toggle between a rendered preview and the source.

Get started with the GitHub App

When you use the GitHub App to work on an issue, artifacts created during the session are automatically attached to that issue. You can also prompt the session to create a specific artifact, such as an implementation plan, root cause analysis, or summary of historical context. Support for creating and viewing HTML artifacts in the GitHub App is coming soon.

Get started with gh issue artifact

The new gh issue artifact command brings issue artifact support to GitHub CLI. You can use the create, edit, list, view, download, and delete commands to manage issue artifacts. Coding agents and developer tools that use gh can also invoke them as part of their workflows.

Artifacts can also be addressed by their GitHub URLs, and Markdown documents support image and video attachments with --attach. For usage details, see the gh issue artifact documentation.

Manage and view artifacts on github.com

Create, edit, and delete artifacts directly from an issue on github.com. You can update an artifact as plans and decisions change while retaining its version history, giving teammates and agents a current source of truth without losing how it evolved.

Each artifact can be linked, making it easy to open, reference, and share.

Share your feedback

Join the GitHub Community to tell us what you think and help shape the public preview.

items.title: GitHub Actions adds multi-cloud compute to improve reliability
items.lede: We’re expanding the infrastructure behind GitHub-hosted runners so your workflows start faster and run more reliably, even during periods of peak demand. GitHub Actions now schedules eligible jobs across a broader, multi-cloud compute pool.
items.text:
We’re expanding the infrastructure behind GitHub-hosted runners so your workflows start faster and run more reliably, even during periods of peak demand. GitHub Actions now schedules eligible jobs across a broader, multi-cloud compute pool. This adds capacity, reduces capacity-related queue times, and improves service resilience. As part of this, eligible Linux jobs may run on Amazon Web Services (AWS) in addition to Microsoft Azure.

Multi-cloud compute will be used for standard 2-core and 4-core Linux runners and compatible 2-core and 4-core larger runners without specialized configurations. This change does not apply to Windows runners or runners with private networking or other specialized configurations.

For customers on GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, and GitHub Team, eligible runners will automatically use multi-cloud compute. Customers on GitHub Enterprise Cloud can opt in by going to Enterprise Settings > Policies > Actions > General > Hosted compute cloud providers and enabling AWS compute.

Editor’s note (November 2, 2026): Corrected the path for opting in.

GitHub Actions automatically schedules eligible jobs across available cloud providers. Your existing runner labels and workflow syntax remain unchanged.

Recommended action: Keep your network allowlists up to date

To get the full benefit of expanded capacity, make sure any IP allowlists or network-based access policies your workflows rely on include all published GitHub Actions IP ranges. Runners in the expanded compute pool use additional outbound IP addresses, so policies that allow only Azure or Microsoft-owned ranges, including Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies, can block connections or authentication from these runners.

This is a rolling change, so we recommend updating your allowlists now, before your workflows begin running in the expanded compute pool.

All GitHub Actions runner IP ranges, including the new ones, are published in the actions array returned by GET https://api.github.com/meta. We recommend keeping your allowlists in sync with this endpoint rather than relying on cloud-provider-specific ranges. See GitHub-hosted runner IP addresses for details.

items.title: Pull request limits: Exempt contributors by age or history
items.lede: Pull request limits help maintainers manage the volume of incoming contributions from people without write access. You can now add exemption rules to decide which contributors can open pull requests beyond the cap, balancing protection from high-volume or low-trust contributions with fewer barriers for established…
items.text:
Pull request limits help maintainers manage the volume of incoming contributions from people without write access. You can now add exemption rules to decide which contributors can open pull requests beyond the cap, balancing protection from high-volume or low-trust contributions with fewer barriers for established community members.

In your organization or repository’s “Moderation” -> “Interaction limits” settings, enable either or both rules and set a threshold:

- Account age: Exempt contributors whose accounts meet or exceed the minimum age you set. This value is in days.

- Merged pull requests: Exempt contributors who have had at least the number of pull requests you set merged in that repository.

A contributor is exempt if they meet at least one enabled rule. You can also manage individual exemptions with the existing exemption list. Repository-level pull request cap settings override the organization’s settings.

If you have any questions or feedback, leave a comment in our Community discussion.

items.title: GitHub Copilot app, Universe releases
items.lede: Work doesn’t always fit in a single repository or session. A feature can span several repositories. A launch plan can pull in specs, designs, and assets without touching a repository at all. Projects in the GitHub Copilot app give that work one home, with its context, agents, and results together.
items.text:
Work doesn’t always fit in a single repository or session. A feature can span several repositories. A launch plan can pull in specs, designs, and assets without touching a repository at all. Projects in the GitHub Copilot app give that work one home, with its context, agents, and results together. Copilot coordinates the work in the background and checks in when it needs you.

Give Copilot a goal

Start a project, describe what you want to get done, and add the context Copilot needs (e.g., repositories, design mocks, Slack threads, or notes from a design meeting). Choose the models and tools for the job. Copilot runs as many agents as the work needs and brings back results (e.g., pull requests) for your review.

Use project automations for repeatable tasks, such as creating a new promo video whenever a feature lands.

For a focused task in a single repository, you can still start a session directly from that repository.

Copilot Projects are now in public preview. You can learn more in the projects documentation.

Handle the work around your code

Use context from connected tools such as Slack and Figma to research a request, draft a specification, or work through a design alongside your code.

You can also generate and edit images using natural language in chat.

Let Copilot work with your desktop apps

Ask Copilot to work through tasks in your desktop apps, such as an expense-report workflow. Computer use—in public preview on macOS and Windows—lets Copilot read app content, click controls, enter or edit text, and navigate across apps, including those without an API, command-line interface, or MCP integration.

Copilot asks for your approval before controlling an app, and your organization can disable the feature through managed settings. To get started, open Settings > Computer Use and turn on Enable Computer Use. On macOS, grant the required Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions.

For more information, see the computer use documentation.

Get started

Download or update the GitHub Copilot app and join the discussion in GitHub Community.

items.title: Connect your tools to Copilot without all the setup
items.lede: The context your agent needs is often outside your repository: a thread in Slack, a design in Figma, an error in Sentry. Until now, giving Copilot that context meant finding a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, setting up a sign-in, and repeating that in each tool you use.
items.text:
The context your agent needs is often outside your repository: a thread in Slack, a design in Figma, an error in Sentry. Until now, giving Copilot that context meant finding a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, setting up a sign-in, and repeating that in each tool you use. GitHub-verified MCP servers, or connectors, are rolling out in public preview. With them, you only have to connect once.

Connect once, use it across Copilot

Pick a service, sign in, and you’re done. There’s no server to find, nothing to install locally, and no credentials to manage. A service you connect in one place works across the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot CLI, VS Code, Copilot in the cloud, and GitHub Mobile. And it works with no extra setup. Copilot keeps you signed in in the background.

Bring in the tools your team already uses

At launch, you can connect 26 services, including Slack, Figma, Notion, Sentry, Linear, Atlassian Rovo, Cloudflare, Vercel, and Work IQ.

To connect a service:

- Copilot app: Open Customize and select Connect on the service you want.

- Copilot CLI: Run /mcp, switch to the Connectors tab, and select Connect on the service you want.

- VS Code: Open the Agents window, go to Customizations, and connect the service you want.

- github.com: Browse services on the Copilot customization page and select the service you want.

Copilot uses a connected service’s tools when they’re relevant to your request. In the Copilot app, you can also set up automations that use a connected service on a schedule, so Copilot does recurring work for you.

Use connected services in Copilot in the cloud

Connected services also work in Copilot in the cloud, whether you start a session on github.com or in the GitHub Mobile app.

Try it

GitHub-verified MCP servers are rolling out in public preview to users on all Copilot plans. To try them with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise, an admin needs to enable the Editor preview features policy for your organization or enterprise. If your enterprise uses an MCP allowlist in managed settings, an admin also needs to add GitHub-verified MCP servers to it. Some services also need to be enabled by an admin on their side, such as allowing Slack MCP access.

Learn more about GitHub-verified MCP servers. Share feedback in our Community discussion.

Happy coding! 💙

items.title: GitHub intelligence puts your code, context, and history to work
items.lede: Agents should understand more than your codebase—they should understand how your team works. Your preferences, repository conventions, skills, and custom instructions guide how changes should be made, while code in related repositories can show how the pieces fit together.
items.text:
Agents should understand more than your codebase—they should understand how your team works. Your preferences, repository conventions, skills, and custom instructions guide how changes should be made, while code in related repositories can show how the pieces fit together. Without that context, agents spend time rediscovering knowledge and can miss your team’s conventions.

GitHub intelligence is the context and learning layer sourced from the graph of GitHub data. It makes this data useful to agents, helping them remember how you work, keep that guidance current, and find the code and development history relevant to the next task. The goal is for agents to build on what you and your team already know, rather than treating every session as a fresh start.

That is the advantage of building where your team’s work already lives. A repository memory can capture why an edge case matters and which test covers it. GitHub intelligence allows agents to use that context, with controls over what they can access.

Three capabilities bring this into your workflow:

- Memory carries knowledge between sessions

- Dreaming keeps the context current

- Code search reaches beyond your checkout.

Availability and settings vary by capability.

Memory: Pick up where you left off

GitHub Copilot Memory is now generally available on paid Copilot plans. Copilot can remember personal preferences and repository conventions across sessions and clients. Memories can be created in the Copilot app, Copilot CLI, VS Code, Copilot cloud agent, Copilot code review, Slack, Teams, and GitHub Mobile.

You can tell Copilot, Remember to start my pull request descriptions with a TL;DR, and it can reuse that preference across Copilot experiences. Repository memories can capture the right test command or how your team expects Copilot to check its work, so you spend less time repeating guidance in each session. Copilot sessions autonomously generate and curate memories, learning from every interaction.

Among the Copilot CLI sessions reviewed during the public preview where the agent used memory, 93% showed better adherence to developer preferences and 42% showed more efficient workflows attributed to the memories included in the session context.

You can interact with memories in the Copilot app, Copilot CLI, and VS Code, or manage personal memories in your Copilot settings, where you can view or delete saved preferences.

Dreaming: Continuous context improvement

Copilot dreaming, now in public preview, reflects on past work to improve future agentic sessions.

Three dream types are currently available:

- Personal memory curation customizes Copilot to your personal preferences by updating memories based on your agent conversations.

- Repository customization manages repository-scoped memories and proposes updates and improvements to existing skills and custom instruction files.

- Code review customization turns recurring accepted code-review feedback into guidance for Copilot code review.

Dreaming can add, update, and remove personal and repository memories. Changes to checked-in skills and instructions are proposed in pull requests for your team to review.

Dreaming is opt-in.

- Individual subscribers: Enable personal curation in your Copilot settings and repository dreams in each repository’s settings. See personal and repository setup.

- Organizations and enterprises: Administrators enable dreaming through Copilot policies. Enterprise administrators can delegate that choice to organization administrators. Repository dreams cover the repositories allowed by Copilot Memory’s repository access settings. Users must also enable personal dreaming in their own Copilot settings.

Dream runs consume AI credits. See the dreaming documentation for prerequisites, setup, and costs.

Code Search: Reach beyond your checkout

Software projects rarely live in a single repository. GitHub code search helps Copilot find relevant code, configuration, schemas, and documentation across related projects and dependencies without needing a local clone.

items.title: Build shared workflows for your team with Copilot Automations
items.lede: Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out, enabling teams to build and maintain AI-powered workflows together.
items.text:
Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out, enabling teams to build and maintain AI-powered workflows together.

With Copilot Automations, you can combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way your team works. Copilot runs autonomously in the cloud, using only the tools you’ve allowed. For example, you could create automations to:

- Reproduce bugs as soon as an issue is opened.

- Capture screenshots of the changes when a pull request is marked as ready.

- Automatically investigate production incidents as soon as they’re detected in your monitoring tool.

Until now, automations have been personal, meaning only you could see and edit them, and they used your identity and AI credits. That works well for automating your own work, like drafting your standup updates, but not for workflows your whole team relies on. Shared automations let your team build and maintain those workflows together.

How shared automations work

- Visible to your team: Everyone with read access to the repository can see a shared automation, and anyone with write access can edit it.

- Billed to the repository owner: AI credits are billed to the organization or user that owns the repository, rather than to the person who created the automation.

- Act as Copilot: Actions on GitHub are attributed to Copilot, rather than to any one user.

- Built to last: Shared automations belong to the repository, so they keep running if the person who created them leaves the team. Change history lets your team see how the tools, triggers, and prompt have evolved.

For shared automations to run in an organization-owned repository, an administrator must enable the “Allow use of Copilot cloud agent billed to the organization” policy.

Create a shared automation

When you create an automation on github.com, the GitHub Copilot app , or Visual Studio Code, choose Shared under Type. You can’t change an automation’s type after you create it. To learn more, see personal and shared automations.

Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out to users on Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans. Availability may vary as the rollout progresses. Once available, you can create automations in any repository where you have write access.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

items.title: New tools, triggers, and cost controls for Copilot Automations
items.lede: With Copilot Automations, you can combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way your team works. Triggers define when your automation runs (e.g., “every day at 9am” or “when a pull request is opened”).
items.text:
With Copilot Automations, you can combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way your team works. Triggers define when your automation runs (e.g., “every day at 9am” or “when a pull request is opened”). Tools define what your automation can do (e.g., “update issue labels” or “create pull request”).

Automations now support:

- New triggers: Start automations from external systems using the API, respond to more GitHub events, and chain automations into multi-step workflows.

- New tools: Choose from 20 new GitHub tools and connect tools from custom MCP servers.

- Cost controls: Set AI credit limits per run, day, week, or month.

More triggers

Trigger automations from external systems using the API

You can now trigger automations with the GitHub REST API, allowing you to connect automations to any external system. For example, you could triage incoming Jira tickets, fix new issues in Sentry, or investigate PagerDuty incidents.

Define your automation with the relevant prompt and tools, then set up a webhook handler to receive events from the external system and call the Trigger an automation API, passing in relevant context.

24 new GitHub triggers

You can now run automations in response to 24 more events across issues, pull requests, discussions, and security alerts:

- Issues: Assigned, sub-issue added, labeled, closed, reopened, and status changed

- Pull requests: Assigned, ready for review, labeled, merge conflict, review submitted, review requested, closed, reopened, converted to draft, review dismissed, and review thread resolved or unresolved

- Discussions: Discussion opened, discussion updated, and comment or reply created

- Security alerts: Code scanning alert created, secret scanning alert created, and Dependabot alert created

Chain automations together

Automations can now trigger other automations, so you can stack them into multi-step workflows. There are two ways to set this up:

- The “Can be triggered by” setting: Each trigger now has a “Can be triggered by” option. It defaults to Only users, but you can set it to Users and Copilot so that events from other automations, such as a pull request opened by Copilot, also fire the trigger.

- Automation run triggers: New Automation run succeeded and Automation run failed triggers let you run one automation after another finishes.

More tools

20 new GitHub tools

You can now allow your automations to:

- Upload image or video attachments to include in issues and pull requests (e.g., screenshots or screen recordings)

- Retry workflow runs

- Merge pull requests

- Update issue and pull request comments

- Mark pull requests as ready for review or convert them to drafts

- Hide and unhide comments, pull request review comments, and pull request reviews

- Remove reactions from issues, pull requests, and comments

- Read discussions, list discussion categories, and comment on discussions

Connect tools from custom MCP servers

Your automations can now use tools provided by MCP servers, so they can work with external systems as well as GitHub. As with GitHub tools, you choose exactly which tools your automation can use.

To configure MCP tools for an automation, add the MCP server in your repository’s settings, then pick the relevant tools from the tool picker when you create your automation.

Cost controls

You can now limit how many AI credits each automation can consume. When you create or edit an automation, you can set any combination of these optional limits:

- Per run: An automation run stops when it reaches this limit.

- Daily, weekly, and monthly: Once the automation reaches one of these limits, new runs won’t start until the period resets.

Automations without limits continue to run as they do today. To get started, see setting AI credit limits on github.com or setting AI credit limits in the GitHub Copilot app.

Copilot Automations is available with Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans. You can create automations in any repository where you have write access.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.
