items.title: Copilot Automations now learn from outcomes and self-improve
items.lede: Copilot Automations can now learn from their outcomes and propose improvements to themselves, helping them produce better results over time.
items.text:
Copilot Automations can now learn from their outcomes and propose improvements to themselves, helping them produce better results over time.

It’s easy to create an automation, but harder to build one you can trust to consistently produce high-quality results. Reviewing its output and improving its prompt by hand takes time. Self-improvement uses feedback from real outcomes on GitHub to make that process easier.

How it works

Your automations leave a trail of signals on GitHub that show how well they’re working. For example:

- An issue triage automation can learn from whether people change the labels it applied.

- A code review automation can learn from whether developers accept its comments.

- A performance optimization automation can learn from whether maintainers merge the pull requests it opens.

Self-improving automations use these signals to propose improvements to their prompts. You stay in control: each proposed change comes to you for review before it’s applied.

How Copilot creates a self-improvement loop

When you ask Copilot to set up a self-improving automation, it can create a group of automations that work together. For example, for a custom code reviewer, Copilot might create:

- A review automation that runs when a pull request is opened, reviews the changes, and posts comments.

- A weekly improvement automation that analyzes how developers responded to those comments and proposes refinements to the review automation.

When the improvement automation proposes a change to the original automation’s prompt, tools, or triggers, GitHub notifies you. You can review and accept or reject the proposed change before it is applied.

To learn more, see about Copilot Automations.

Copilot Automations is available with Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

items.title: Create and manage Copilot Automations in Visual Studio Code
items.lede: Copilot Automations in Visual Studio Code can now run in the cloud. You can create and manage cloud automations from the Agents window without leaving your editor.
items.text:
Copilot Automations in Visual Studio Code can now run in the cloud. You can create and manage cloud automations from the Agents window without leaving your editor.

With Copilot Automations, you combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way you work. Pick when an automation should run and what it is allowed to do, then write a prompt telling Copilot how to complete the task.

Visual Studio Code already supports personal automations that run locally on a schedule. With cloud automations, you can now:

- Run personal scheduled automations even when Visual Studio Code is closed: Cloud automations keep running when your computer is asleep or turned off, so recurring work does not depend on your machine being available.

- Set up personal automations that run in response to events on GitHub: Act automatically when activity happens in your repository (e.g., an issue being assigned to you or a pull request being opened).

- Build shared workflows in the cloud with your team: Create automations visible to everyone with access to the repository and act as Copilot.

To get started, update to Visual Studio Code 1.144 and enable the chat.automations.cloud.enabled setting. You’ll find automations in the Automations tab in the Agents window. To learn more, see “Create and manage agent automations” in the Visual Studio Code docs.

Copilot Automations is available with Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

items.title: Agent Merge watches and fixes pull requests in the cloud
items.lede: With Agent Merge, Copilot watches your pull request and automatically fixes blockers, (e.g., failing Actions workflows and merge conflicts) that stand in the way of getting your pull request merged.
items.text:
With Agent Merge, Copilot watches your pull request and automatically fixes blockers, (e.g., failing Actions workflows and merge conflicts) that stand in the way of getting your pull request merged.

Already available in the GitHub Copilot app and Visual Studio Code, Agent Merge is now integrated into pull requests on GitHub. This helps you get your pull requests merged faster wherever you work.

To get started, select Watch and fix in your pull request’s merge box. You can choose whether Copilot should fix failing Actions workflows, resolve merge conflicts, or both. When a selected blocker appears, Copilot starts working in a cloud development environment to fix it.

Want Copilot to unblock every pull request you open? You can enable Agent Merge by default for all your pull requests from your Copilot settings.

You can combine Agent Merge with auto-merge. This way Copilot gets and keeps your pull request ready to merge, and GitHub merges it as soon as all requirements are met.

Agent Merge in the cloud is available to users with a paid Copilot plan, subject to applicable organization and enterprise policies. To learn more, see the GitHub Docs.

If you have any questions or feedback, leave a comment in our Community discussion.

items.title: Copilot code review: Merge with confidence with Max and approvals
items.lede: GitHub Copilot code review now offers its most thorough review and can approve your pull request when it’s ready to merge. The new Max review effort level is now in public preview, and Copilot approvals are generally available.
items.text:
GitHub Copilot code review now offers its most thorough review and can approve your pull request when it’s ready to merge. The new Max review effort level is now in public preview, and Copilot approvals are generally available. Together, they turn a high-quality review into a high-confidence approval, so you can merge with confidence and spend less time waiting on review.

These features are available with Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans.

🚀 Max: The most thorough review from Copilot

Some pull requests carry more risk than others, like a change to authentication logic or to a shared library that several services depend on. Max is built for those types of changes. It joins Lite and Balanced as a third review effort level and runs several independent review agents across models from different providers. Each model has its own strengths and blind spots, so combining them helps catch issues a single model might miss. An aggregation agent then reconciles their findings, resolves disagreements, and double-checks accuracy before combining everything into a single review.

The result is Copilot’s broadest coverage, especially on critical issues, while keeping noise low.

Choose Max when you want the deepest analysis Copilot can provide before you merge. Because Max does more work on each review, it takes longer and uses more AI credits than Lite or Balanced.

✅ Approvals: From review to merge-ready

Copilot approvals, previously available in public preview, are now generally available.

Copilot code review acts as both a reviewer and an approver. Every review includes an approval assessment in the pull request overview comment that tells you whether Copilot considers the pull request ready to merge. When approvals are turned on, Copilot can approve the pull request, and that approval counts toward your repository’s required approvals.

Copilot’s approval behaves like a human reviewer’s approval. If new commits are pushed after Copilot approves, the approval is dismissed, and you can request a new review to get a fresh approval.

🤝 Better reviews, better approvals

Copilot’s approval assessment builds on the findings from its review. Pair Max with approvals on the repositories where a missed issue costs the most, and Copilot’s sign-off reflects the most thorough review it can provide.

⚙️ Configure and control Max

You can select Max for a single pull request from the “Reviewers” bar or set it as the default review effort for a repository, organization, or enterprise. Each level can override the one above it.

Enterprise, organization, and repository admins can optionally set a maximum review effort level to decide where Max is available. Review effort levels above the selected maximum will not be available to use within the enterprise, organization, or repository.

⚙️ Configure approvals

Approvals are off by default. Admins can turn them on at the enterprise, organization, or repository level, and repository admins can choose which file paths Copilot is allowed to approve.

To get started with configuring Max effort level and approvals, see Configuring code review by GitHub Copilot.

Share your feedback in the Copilot code review community discussion.

links.text: Configuring code review by GitHub Copilot

items.title: GitHub Enterprise now includes access to GitHub Copilot
items.lede: Enterprises working with a GitHub or Microsoft account team can now get Copilot included with GitHub Enterprise for every licensed user. Previously, you had to manage two things: how many Copilot seats you were paying for and how much AI usage those users consumed.
items.text:
Enterprises working with a GitHub or Microsoft account team can now get Copilot included with GitHub Enterprise for every licensed user. Previously, you had to manage two things: how many Copilot seats you were paying for and how much AI usage those users consumed. With Copilot included in the platform, usage against your enterprise budget is the primary thing to manage.

Self-serve availability is coming in stages, and current self-serve subscriptions are unaffected. Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise remain available.

Users in your enterprise account who do not hold a GitHub Enterprise license get the same Copilot access through Copilot Standalone, at $10 per user per month.

Copilot access through GitHub Enterprise and Copilot Standalone has the same features and models as Copilot Enterprise but does not include monthly AI credits per seat.

What you manage

AI usage is metered from the first request against your enterprise budget, using the policies, alerts, and attribution you already have. There is no included usage allowance to track or top up. To learn more, review our documentation on Copilot billing for enterprises.

- Code completion and next edit suggestions keep working even with no budget available.

- Copilot Chat, Copilot code review, and Copilot in the cloud require available budget to use.

- An exhausted budget never removes access. The seat and the features that don’t need budget stay.

Availability

- If you work with a GitHub or Microsoft account team: Available now for GitHub Enterprise Cloud. Talk to your sales team about setting up a new enterprise account on this model or transitioning an existing enterprise account.

- If you manage your own subscription: Currently unavailable. We are opening this to self-serve customers in stages and will share dates in the coming weeks. Your current subscription is unaffected.

- Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise: Both remain available to purchase for new and existing enterprises.

To learn more, check out our updated documentation on Copilot access.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

items.title: GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles are generally available
items.lede: You can now use GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles in general availability on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans.
items.text:
You can now use GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles in general availability on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. Lockfiles let you keep readable tag and branch references in your workflows while running the exact commits you locked, even if those references move.

This release brings the capabilities introduced in the public preview to general availability:

- Lock your dependencies: Use the gh actions-lock extension for the GitHub CLI to generate .github/workflows/actions.lock for actions and their transitive dependencies.

- Adopt locking gradually: Onboard workflows individually. GitHub Actions requires each dependency of an onboarded workflow to be in the lockfile and runs its recorded commit.

- Keep updates in sync: When Dependabot opens a version update for an action in an onboarded workflow, it also regenerates the matching lockfile entry in the same pull request, without additional configuration.

- Require lockfile: Enterprise, organization, and repository administrators can use the Require lockfile policy to enforce adoption.

- Check for stale lockfiles: Verify that your lockfile is up to date without modifying files, including in a CI check.

Lockfiles help protect against unexpected dependency changes, but they don’t determine whether a dependency is safe. Review dependencies before locking them.

Get started

Install the extension from the gh-actions-lock repository, then review and commit the generated lockfile and workflow changes. See workflow dependency lockfiles in GitHub Docs for details and setup instructions.

Share feedback in the community discussion or report an issue with the extension.

links.text: report an issue with the extension

items.title: Moderate role for GitHub Issues generally available
items.lede: Update (October 28, 2026): The Moderate role feature is not yet available.
items.text:
Update (October 28, 2026): The Moderate role feature is not yet available.

The Moderate role will be available in the coming weeks.

We’ve introduced a new Moderate role that allows you to moderate and edit issues without granting access to code.

Below are the actions you can perform with the Moderate role.

Content editing

- Edit issues you didn’t author, including issue titles, bodies, and comments

Moderation

- Transfer issues between repositories. This requires Moderate role access or above on both the source and destination repository.

- Hide and unhide issue comments

- Lock and unlock conversation on an issue

- Comment on locked issues

Managing metadata

- Create and edit issue labels

- Create and edit issue milestones

- Create and edit discussion categories

Check out the documentation on repository roles for more details.

Join the discussion and share your feedback within GitHub Community.

items.title: GitHub Copilot SDK is becoming Microsoft Copilot SDK
items.lede: We’re transitioning GitHub Copilot SDK to Microsoft Copilot SDK.
items.text:
We’re transitioning GitHub Copilot SDK to Microsoft Copilot SDK.

What began as the SDK for the GitHub Copilot harness is becoming the programmable interface for the Microsoft Copilot harness, the shared agent foundation used across Microsoft and GitHub products. This evolution reflects our broader goal to enable developers to build and customize agent experiences using the same core foundation that powers our own products, while retaining control over their prompts, tools, policies, and application experiences.

As part of this transition, we have begun updating the SDK repository to reflect the upcoming move to the Microsoft organization and begun updating branding and documentation. The migration will happen in phases, so existing package names, namespaces, and some documentation may continue to reference GitHub Copilot SDK during the transition.

This announcement is to share the SDK’s direction and expanded role. No immediate changes are required for existing users.

Support for the Copilot SDK remains the same. For more information: copilot-sdk/SUPPORT.md

links.text: upcoming move to the Microsoft organization

items.title: Repository plugin defaults and enterprise plugin controls generally available
items.lede: Repository plugin defaults and enterprise-managed plugin controls are now generally available in VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. Trusted repositories can install and enable default plugins for contributors.
items.text:
Repository plugin defaults and enterprise-managed plugin controls are now generally available in VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. Trusted repositories can install and enable default plugins for contributors. Enterprises can require plugins, block plugins, and restrict installation to approved marketplaces.

As a repository maintainer, you can define a plugin marketplace and default plugins so contributors don’t have to repeat setup for each project. Contributors can turn off repository defaults where policy permits.

As an enterprise administrator, you can supply approved marketplaces and require or block plugins through managed settings. Required plugins are automatically installed and enabled, and users can’t disable them. Managed settings take precedence over repository and personal choices.

Repository defaults are available to individual Copilot users and users with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise.

Managed controls are available on GitHub Enterprise Cloud for users with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise licenses issued by the enterprise or one of its organizations.

Learn more about plugins for GitHub Copilot.

items.title: Webhook IP ranges added to the Meta API
items.lede: We’re adding IP ranges for GitHub webhook deliveries on github.com. The Meta API now includes these additional ranges in the hooks field.
items.text:
We’re adding IP ranges for GitHub webhook deliveries on github.com. The Meta API now includes these additional ranges in the hooks field.

If you maintain a static network allowlist for incoming webhook deliveries, add these CIDR prefixes alongside your existing webhook IP ranges to avoid rejecting deliveries:

- 9.234.98.160/28

- 9.234.98.176/28

- 9.234.106.48/28

If you already keep your allowlist up to date using the Meta API, no changes are needed for these additions.

These ranges apply to webhook deliveries on github.com across all plans, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

You can retrieve the current webhook IP ranges using the Meta API and follow the webhook delivery best practices.

items.title: pull_request_target blocked by default December 2
items.lede: Starting December 2, 2026, GitHub Actions will block pull_request_target events by default in all public repositories, unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. Enforcement was previously scheduled for November 2, 2026.
items.text:
Starting December 2, 2026, GitHub Actions will block pull_request_target events by default in all public repositories, unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. Enforcement was previously scheduled for November 2, 2026.

GitHub introduced this default rule through workflow execution protections. The rule initially runs in evaluate mode, so you can see which workflow runs it would block before enforcement begins.

Private and internal repositories aren’t affected.

Why we’re making this change

pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository and can access its secrets. If a workflow executes untrusted code from a fork, that code could compromise your pipeline or steal secrets. The default rule helps reduce this risk while letting you explicitly allow workflows that depend on the trigger.

Brownout schedule

Before permanent enforcement begins on December 2, 2026, we’ll temporarily enforce the default protection during two scheduled brownouts. These windows will help you identify affected workflows and update your policies before enforcement becomes permanent.

Date |
Time (UTC) |

November 9, 2026 |
16:00–18:00 |

November 16, 2026 |
16:00–18:00 |

During each window, pull_request_target workflow attempts blocked by the default rule in affected public repositories will create failed runs with an error annotation; the workflows won’t execute. After each window, the default rule will return to evaluate mode, allowing workflows to run with warnings. Private and internal repositories aren’t affected.

Prepare your workflows

Before the first brownout on November 9, use Insights to see which workflow runs the rule would block. From there, you have two options:

- Keep the default rule in place to block pull_request_target.

- Explicitly allow pull_request_target in an applicable Actions event policy if your workflows depend on it. Use workflow file targeting to allow specific workflows.

See how to control workflow execution to configure your policies.

This change applies to public repositories on GitHub Free, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud, not GitHub Enterprise Server.

items.title: Security risk assessments include repository protection status
items.lede: The GitHub code security risk assessment and secret risk assessment now show whether findings are in protected or unprotected repositories, helping you identify where to extend your security coverage.
items.text:
The GitHub code security risk assessment and secret risk assessment now show whether findings are in protected or unprotected repositories, helping you identify where to extend your security coverage.

Organization admins and security managers can start an assessment by going to Assessments under their organization’s Security tab.

This improvement is available in GitHub Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Team. It will be available for the secret risk assessment in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Read more in the code security risk assessment documentation and secret risk assessment documentation.

items.title: GitHub Desktop adds short-lived authentication tokens
items.lede: When you sign in to GitHub Desktop 3.6.10 or later, eligible accounts can now use short-lived, automatically refreshing authentication tokens.
items.text:
When you sign in to GitHub Desktop 3.6.10 or later, eligible accounts can now use short-lived, automatically refreshing authentication tokens.

Short-lived access tokens reduce how long a leaked token can be used. Desktop automatically refreshes them for GitHub API requests and Git operations, keeping token renewal out of your everyday workflow.

We’re rolling this out gradually on github.com, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud, so it isn’t available to everyone yet. This token rollout doesn’t include GitHub Enterprise Server. Existing sessions stay signed in after upgrading, and existing tokens aren’t automatically migrated. Short-lived tokens are issued during sign-in as the rollout reaches your installation.

Get the latest version of GitHub Desktop and see the GitHub Desktop authentication documentation for sign-in instructions. Share feedback or report a problem in the GitHub Desktop repository, or contact GitHub Support.

items.title: CodeQL 2.27.3 adds Python 3.15 features and JSON data extensions
items.lede: CodeQL is the static analysis engine behind GitHub code scanning, which finds and remediates security issues in your code. We’ve recently released CodeQL 2.27.3. It supports new Python 3.15 language features, adds JSON syntax for data extensions, adds C23 bit-precise integers, and includes accuracy improvements across…
items.text:
CodeQL is the static analysis engine behind GitHub code scanning, which finds and remediates security issues in your code. We’ve recently released CodeQL 2.27.3. It supports new Python 3.15 language features, adds JSON syntax for data extensions, adds C23 bit-precise integers, and includes accuracy improvements across languages.

Language and framework support

CodeQL CLI

- Data extension files now support JSON syntax, using the same structure as YAML data extensions. Java-style comments (// ... and /* ... */) also work. CodeQL parses files with the .json extension as JSON and continues to parse all other files as YAML.

- We’ve added an opt-in ai threat model for LLM-generated data. It doesn’t include any built-in source models, so you can define your own sources with data extensions.

Python

- The Python extractor now supports Python 3.15 syntax, including unary plus in match literal patterns and Unicode 17 identifiers.

- We’ve added support for the new frozendict and sentinel builtins introduced in Python 3.15, including data flow modeling for frozendict construction.

C/C++

- We’ve added support for C23 bit-precise integers (_BitInt(N)).

- We’ve added flow summaries for the BlazingMQ BloombergLP::bmqa::Message and MessageProperties classes and their iterators.

C#

- We’ve added support for data flow through positional patterns in is expressions and switch cases.

- When you configure private registries, CodeQL now passes the required proxy and certificate environment variables to the NuGet CLI.

Ruby

- CodeQL now treats Grape::API request sub-accessors as remote flow sources. These include body.read, body.string, params, GET, POST, cookies, env, query_string, and path_info.

Query changes

C/C++

- The cpp/resource-not-released-in-destructor query now recognizes resources released through local aliases, reducing false positives.

C#

- The cs/simplifiable-boolean-expression query now produces fewer false positives when type information is incomplete.

Java/Kotlin

- The java/ssrf and java/unvalidated-url-redirection queries now recognize case-insensitive comparisons of URI.getHost() with fixed allowlist entries. They also recognize these checks when code stores the host in a local variable, which reduces false positives.

Python

- The py/xxe, py/xml-bomb, and py/nosql-injection queries now respect your configured threat model when selecting untrusted data sources. By default, they still use remote flow sources. These queries now also include sources you model with data extensions.

Breaking changes

- GitHub Actions: The GitHub Actions control flow graph (CFG) now uses the shared CFG library. If your custom queries rely on specific CFG nodes, edges, or basic block boundaries, you may need to update them. We’ve removed the legacy Completion classes, so use CFG edge labels such as DirectSuccessor, BooleanSuccessor, and ReturnSuccessor instead.

For a full list of changes, please refer to the complete changelog for version 2.27.3. Every new version of CodeQL is automatically deployed to users of GitHub code scanning on github.com. The new functionality in CodeQL 2.27.3 will also be included in GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) 3.24 release. If you use an older version of GHES, you can manually upgrade your CodeQL version.

items.title: GitHub Copilot is now available in JetBrains Air
items.lede: You can now delegate coding tasks, guide execution, and review results with GitHub Copilot in JetBrains Air. The integration uses the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) and supports tasks in your JetBrains IDE or in the cloud.
items.text:
You can now delegate coding tasks, guide execution, and review results with GitHub Copilot in JetBrains Air. The integration uses the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) and supports tasks in your JetBrains IDE or in the cloud.

Use Copilot in Air alongside the GitHub Copilot plugin and choose the workflow that works best for you. For a comparison and FAQ, see GitHub Copilot in JetBrains Air.

What’s new

- GitHub Copilot in Air’s agent picker: Select GitHub Copilot and use your existing Copilot subscription for coding tasks.

- Parallel work and in-context review: Track multiple agent sessions, use project context and IDE tools, and review changes alongside your code.

- Cloud tasks on your GitHub Copilot subscription: Run Copilot in isolated cloud environments through Air Teams, from your IDE or browser. Tasks use your Copilot plan rather than JetBrains AI credits.

Get started

For local tasks, install Air in your JetBrains IDE, select GitHub Copilot, and connect your GitHub Copilot account.

For cloud tasks, you’ll need a JetBrains account in an Air Teams-enabled business organization, a GitHub Copilot subscription, and Copilot enabled by your Air administrator. There are two ways to run cloud tasks:

- Browser: Open Air in your browser, connect GitHub under Settings > VCS Providers, and create a task. Choose your repository and remote branch, select GitHub Copilot, and send your prompt.

- IDE: Use the Air plugin in your JetBrains IDE and select Cloud from the environment selector.

Where Copilot cloud tasks run

When you run a GitHub Copilot cloud task through JetBrains Air, Copilot works in a Docker container on a fresh virtual machine. All traffic passes through a proxy, and no state carries over between tasks. Copilot can build, test, and install packages without modifying your local environment. For more information, see Cloud agent sandboxing in Air.

Cloud task considerations

- Subscription checks: Connecting GitHub Copilot to Air does not request GitHub Copilot permissions. Air may only verify subscription or credit availability when the cloud environment starts. If your subscription or credits are unavailable, the task fails and an error appears in the session.

- Plan selection: You cannot choose whether an individual task uses your personal GitHub Copilot plan or your organization’s plan.

- Usage visibility: Air’s governance and analytics features do not include Copilot usage.

- Administrative controls: Air administrators can disable GitHub Copilot through a governance policy, but cannot set Copilot spending limits within Air.

Share your feedback

Share your thoughts through in-product feedback, our feedback repository, or the private survey.

items.title: Look up a resource’s cost center with the GitHub REST API
items.lede: You can now use the GitHub REST API to find which cost center a user, organization, repository, or enterprise team belongs to. Previously, you had to list every cost center and scan its resources.
items.text:
You can now use the GitHub REST API to find which cost center a user, organization, repository, or enterprise team belongs to. Previously, you had to list every cost center and scan its resources.

Pass the resource type and name to the new endpoint. The response includes the cost center’s ID and name. If the resource doesn’t belong to a cost center, the memberships array is empty.

Access depends on your role:

- Enterprise owners, billing managers, and GitHub Apps with read access to enterprise billing can look up any resource in the enterprise.

- Organization owners and users with custom roles that include read access to enterprise billing can only look up the resources and cost centers they can already see.

To get started, see Get cost center membership for a resource in the REST API documentation.

links.text: Get cost center membership for a resource

items.title: Dependabot version updates support Agent Package Manager
items.lede: You can now keep your AI agent skills, prompts, and instructions up to date with Dependabot version updates for Agent Package Manager (APM).
items.text:
You can now keep your AI agent skills, prompts, and instructions up to date with Dependabot version updates for Agent Package Manager (APM).

Dependabot opens pull requests to update supported git dependencies declared in apm.yml and regenerates apm.lock.yaml when it’s present. This support covers version updates, not security updates.

Get started

Add an apm entry to your .github/dependabot.yml file, specify the directory containing apm.yml, and choose an update schedule.

APM support is generally available on github.com for all GitHub plans and will be available in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Learn more

- Configuring Dependabot version updates

- Supported APM dependencies and update behavior

- Community discussion on APM support

links.text: Supported APM dependencies and update behavior

items.title: BYOK and enterprise custom models in the Copilot usage API
items.lede: The Copilot usage metrics API now shows bring your own key (BYOK) usage across GitHub Copilot, so you can separate it from Copilot-hosted model usage. Reports cover two kinds of BYOK:
items.text:
The Copilot usage metrics API now shows bring your own key (BYOK) usage across GitHub Copilot, so you can separate it from Copilot-hosted model usage. Reports cover two kinds of BYOK:

- Local BYOK is configured by developers in their client. Requests go from Copilot CLI or the GitHub Copilot app directly to the developer’s provider key or local model. Find it in used_local_byok, totals_by_local_byok, and active local BYOK user counts.

- Enterprise custom models are configured by admins in GitHub settings, and requests route through GitHub to your provider. Find them with is_custom_enterprise_model in totals_by_client.

Both appear in enterprise and organization reports, at the user and aggregate level, in 1-day and 28-day reports.

Local BYOK

Local BYOK covers a developer’s own provider key and local models served by tools such as Ollama, Foundry Local, LM Studio, and llama-server.

- used_local_byok: Whether a user made at least one local BYOK request in Copilot CLI or the Copilot app that day. Appears in user-level reports.

- totals_by_local_byok: Session, request, prompt, and token counts, broken out by byok_kind (local_managed, local_user, local_auto, or remote_user) and surface (copilot_cli or copilot_app). Appears in user-level and aggregate reports.

- daily_active_local_byok_users, weekly_active_local_byok_users, and monthly_active_local_byok_users: Distinct users with local BYOK activity for the day, calendar week, and calendar month. Appears in aggregate reports.

Enterprise custom models

- Added is_custom_enterprise_model, a boolean on each totals_by_client[].totals_by_model[] entry. Its value is true when the request used a custom model configured for your enterprise or organization. GitHub observes these requests server-side, so the field covers every client, including IDEs.

- A model used both as a Copilot-hosted model and as a custom model appears as two entries, so the counts stay separate.

- Custom model entries include real request and token counts.

Why this matters

BYOK usage used to blend into Copilot-hosted totals, because local and custom models often share names with Copilot models. Now you can:

- Govern BYOK: See who sends requests to their own provider keys, local models, or enterprise custom models, and check that against your BYOK policy.

- Understand spend: Separate Copilot-hosted usage from usage billed by your own provider or run on free local models, so cost per user reflects what Copilot actually serves.

- See across all tools: Get one view of AI usage in your enterprise, whichever model or provider your developers choose.

- Compare efficiency: Group users by BYOK or custom model usage and compare them against the Copilot usage metrics you already track.

Important notes

- No change to existing totals: BYOK usage is already counted. Local BYOK is a subset of totals_by_cli and totals_by_copilot_app, and custom model usage is already in totals_by_client. Existing totals are unchanged.

- Lower bound for local BYOK: Local BYOK fields rely on client telemetry, so they undercount when telemetry is disabled. Token counts can also undercount because some local providers don’t report token usage. Enterprise custom model counts are observed server-side and don’t have this limitation.

- Model names: Custom model names use the existing model name normalization, so unrecognized names appear as unknown. Local BYOK usage isn’t broken out by model name.

- No backfill: Report days before this release don’t include is_custom_enterprise_model.

- Access: Available to enterprise owners, enterprise billing managers, organization owners, and anyone with a custom organization or enterprise role that grants the View Copilot Metrics permission. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.

Visit the Copilot usage metrics API documentation to get started.

items.title: GitHub Copilot is now available in Xcode’s coding assistant
items.lede: You can now work with GitHub Copilot directly in Xcode’s built-in coding assistant, bringing Copilot into your native Xcode workflow. The integration is now in public preview, available starting with Xcode 27.3 beta.
items.text:
You can now work with GitHub Copilot directly in Xcode’s built-in coding assistant, bringing Copilot into your native Xcode workflow. The integration is now in public preview, available starting with Xcode 27.3 beta.

Share your feedback

Help us improve the experience by sharing your feedback in the GitHub Copilot for Xcode repository or through Apple Feedback Assistant.

items.title: CodeQL 2.27.4 improves accuracy and query metadata
items.lede: CodeQL is the static analysis engine behind GitHub code scanning, which finds and remediates security issues in your code. We’ve recently released CodeQL 2.27.4 with query accuracy improvements across several languages, stronger security checks when you bundle or publish a pack, and corrections to query metadata.
items.text:
CodeQL is the static analysis engine behind GitHub code scanning, which finds and remediates security issues in your code. We’ve recently released CodeQL 2.27.4 with query accuracy improvements across several languages, stronger security checks when you bundle or publish a pack, and corrections to query metadata.

Query changes

Java/Kotlin

- The java/log-injection query now recognizes additional sanitizers and sanitizer guards from the JDK, Apache Commons Lang and Text, Guava, OWASP Java Encoder, and Spring Framework.

- Path-injection queries now recognize additional substring guards and string replacement and removal operations from Apache Commons Lang and Guava.

Rust

- We have reduced false positives in the rust/uncontrolled-allocation-size, rust/log-injection, and rust/cleartext-logging queries.

C/C++

- The cpp/suspicious-pointer-scaling query no longer reports intentional pointer arithmetic on std::byte* buffers.

- The cpp/unused-local-variable and cpp/unused-static-variable queries no longer report variables marked with [[maybe_unused]].

CWE metadata changes

CodeQL no longer applies the CWE-730 tag to the following queries:

- C#: cs/redos and cs/regex-injection.

- Java/Kotlin: java/redos, java/polynomial-redos, and java/regex-injection.

- JavaScript/TypeScript: js/redos, js/polynomial-redos, js/regex-injection, js/regex-injection-more-sources, js/server-crash, and js/loop-bound-injection.

- Python: py/redos, py/polynomial-redos, and py/regex-injection.

- Ruby: rb/redos, rb/polynomial-redos, and rb/regexp-injection.

- Swift: swift/redos and swift/regex-injection.

This was initially reported in CodeQL issue #22318; thank you to @wiggin15 for the feedback.

CodeQL CLI

- The CLI now writes Java virtual machine warnings and initialization errors to standard error, so they won’t interfere with JSON or other machine-readable output.

- When you bundle or publish a pack, the CLI checks whether each file remains inside the pack root after resolving symbolic links. It omits files that resolve outside the root and displays a warning.

For full details, see the CodeQL 2.27.4 changelog. GitHub automatically deploys every new CodeQL version to users of GitHub code scanning on github.com. The new functionality in CodeQL 2.27.4 will also be included in the GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) 3.24 release. If you use an older version of GHES, you can manually upgrade your CodeQL version.

items.title: New pull request overview page in public preview
items.lede: On a long pull request, checking what’s blocking often means scrolling past dozens of comments and timeline events just to reach the merge box. And once you’re there, you still need to work out what to do next. As people need to review more and more pull requests, time spent scrolling adds up.
items.text:
On a long pull request, checking what’s blocking often means scrolling past dozens of comments and timeline events just to reach the merge box. And once you’re there, you still need to work out what to do next. As people need to review more and more pull requests, time spent scrolling adds up. So we’ve begun to rethink the entire experience, beginning with addressing a familiar challenge: finding what’s blocking progress and determining what to do next.

Today, we’re introducing the Overview page as an opt-in public preview, with rollout continuing through the weekend. It brings merge status and next available actions to the top of the page in a compact readiness summary. It’s the first step toward making pull requests easier to follow as code, conversations, and reviews evolve.

The merge box, distilled

We’re starting with the merge box, the place developers go to see whether a pull request can move forward. Rather than just moving it higher, we’ve also redesigned it to show the same information in less than half the space.

- Explore the supporting signals: A compact view of checks, comments, and approvals keeps the context nearby without making every detail compete for attention.

- Address what’s blocking: Take action to move the pull request forward, such as updating your branch.

- See if it’s ready to merge: Check merge readiness and merge when requirements are met.

Start with the summary, then follow the detail that matters to your next step (e.g., get to failing checks, see who still needs to approve, or open the relevant comments).

Keep your place. Focus your attention.

This first preview also introduces more ways to catch up on activity and focus the conversation so you can spend less time finding your place.

- Narrow the conversation: Filter for unresolved conversations or comments you wrote to find open questions or follow up on your feedback.

- Read the latest comments first: Sort comments from newest to oldest instead of starting with the earliest discussion.

- Catch up on activity: Use the summary in the upper-right to find review comments, review requests, and other updates.

You can also mark a draft ready for review or close a pull request from the header, with available actions depending on your permissions.

Try the new overview

To join, select the ✨ Try the Overview page button in the header. We’re opening this preview early so you can try the new direction on your own pull requests and help shape what comes next. You can use the same menu to return to the classic overview during the preview.

Help shape what comes next

This preview is very much a starting point, not the finished pull request experience. Try it on your next pull request. What is easier to find? Where do you still lose context? What sends you back to the classic overview?

Share your feedback and report issues in the overview preview feedback discussion.

items.title: Usage metrics API flags telemetry and version gaps
items.lede: The Copilot usage metrics API now shows which users are missing client telemetry or are running IDE or extension versions below the usage metrics minimums. New per-user fields appear in enterprise and organization user reports, and daily affected-user counts appear in enterprise and organization reports.
items.text:
The Copilot usage metrics API now shows which users are missing client telemetry or are running IDE or extension versions below the usage metrics minimums. New per-user fields appear in enterprise and organization user reports, and daily affected-user counts appear in enterprise and organization reports.

What’s new

- client_telemetry_present: Whether client telemetry was received for the user that day. false means Copilot saw the user’s activity, but no usage events arrived from their editor.

- usage_metrics_requirements: Lists each of the user’s IDEs and Copilot extensions as met, unmet, or unknown against the minimum supported versions.

- missing_client_telemetry_user_count: The number of users that day with client_telemetry_present set to false.

- below_usage_metrics_minimum_user_count: The number of users that day with at least one IDE or extension below the minimum version.

Why this matters

Users without client telemetry still count as active, but their reports lack detail such as lines of code, feature breakdowns, and model breakdowns. Common causes include outdated editors or extensions, disabled IDE telemetry, and proxies or firewalls that block events. These fields show how many users are affected and who to follow up with. This way you can close gaps without opening a support ticket.

Important notes

- Scope: User fields appear in enterprise and organization user reports (1-day and 28-day). Counts appear in enterprise and organization 1-day reports and in each day_totals entry of 28-day reports.

- Access: These fields are available to enterprise owners, enterprise billing managers, organization owners, and anyone with a custom organization or enterprise role that grants the View Copilot Metrics permission. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.

- Daily counts: Each count covers a single day. A user can be counted in both missing_client_telemetry_user_count and below_usage_metrics_minimum_user_count, so don’t add the two counts together. Don’t add counts across days to count unique users.

- Independent signals: A user can meet every version minimum and still be missing telemetry (e.g., they’re behind a proxy).

- Unavailable values: Null or omitted values mean the data is unavailable, not false or zero. Days before this release have no values.

Visit the Copilot usage metrics API documentation to get started.

items.title: Usage metrics API adds code review details and addressed rate
items.lede: The enterprise and organization repository-level Copilot usage metrics reports now show what happens to Copilot code review feedback. A new copilot_code_review object on each repos-1-day row reports how many Copilot-reviewed pull requests merged without a later change request from a person and how many Copilot code…
items.text:
The enterprise and organization repository-level Copilot usage metrics reports now show what happens to Copilot code review feedback. A new copilot_code_review object on each repos-1-day row reports how many Copilot-reviewed pull requests merged without a later change request from a person and how many Copilot code review comments developers acted on. With these you can track an addressed rate per repository.

What’s new

- total_comments_evaluated: The number of Copilot code review comments checked to see whether the developer acted on them.

- total_comments_addressed: The number of evaluated comments the developer acted on, whether by applying the suggestion, asking Copilot to make the fix, editing the code, or replying that the fix will come in a later pull request. Divide by total_comments_evaluated for the addressed rate.

- review_comments_by_severity, review_comments_by_review_tier, review_comments_by_comment_type, and review_comments_by_customization: Both counts broken down by severity (e.g., high, medium, low), review tier (e.g., lite, balanced, max), comment type (e.g., bug, security, or custom for your repository’s own coding guidelines), and customization (e.g., custom instructions, skills, MCP servers, or none).

- total_merged_no_human_change_request_after_review: The number of merged pull requests that Copilot code review reviewed where no person requested changes after Copilot’s first review.

Why this matters

The existing pull_requests fields show how often Copilot code review runs and how often someone clicks to apply a suggestion, but developers act on most feedback in other ways. These fields show whether developers act on Copilot code review feedback in each repository, which kinds of comments land, whether custom instructions, skills, and MCP servers make a difference, and whether reviewers still request changes after Copilot reviews.

Important notes

- Scope: Present on every row of the enterprise and organization repos-1-day reports. Counts are 0 and arrays are empty when a repository had no Copilot code review activity that day.

- Counted on merge: Comments are evaluated when their pull request merges, so they count on the merge day, not the day Copilot posted them.

- Bot pull requests: Copilot usually doesn’t evaluate comments on pull requests opened by bots, such as Copilot cloud agent. total_merged_no_human_change_request_after_review still includes those pull requests.

- Different from suggestion counts: pull_requests.total_copilot_applied_suggestions counts only ready-to-apply suggestions that someone applied. The new counts include every evaluated comment and count them as addressed however the developer acted on them.

- Access: Enterprise owners, enterprise billing managers, organization owners, and anyone with a custom organization or enterprise role that grants the View Copilot Metrics permission can access these reports. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.

Visit the Copilot usage metrics API documentation to get started.

items.title: Secret scanning upgrades detectors, adds SpaceX as partner
items.lede: This update expands secret scanning’s detection coverage:
items.text:
This update expands secret scanning’s detection coverage:

- New partner: SpaceX is now a secret scanning partner.

- New detector: GitHub now detects starlink_public_api_v2_secret.

- Upgraded detectors: Alibaba, AWS, Google, OpenVSX, Pydantic Services, and Tencent detectors include additional false-positive filtering.

New secret scanning partners

The following provider joined the secret scanning partnership program. When one of their secrets is found in a public repository, GitHub forwards it to the partner so they can revoke or rotate the credential before it can be abused.

Provider |
Secret type |

SpaceX |
starlink_public_api_v2_secret |

Detectors added

Secret scanning now automatically detects the following new secret type in your repositories.

Provider |
Secret type |

SpaceX |
starlink_public_api_v2_secret |

Partner secrets are automatically reported to the secret issuer when found in public repositories through the secret scanning partnership program. User secrets generate secret scanning alerts when found in public or private repositories.

False positives reduced

The following detector improvements reduce false-positive matches for supported secrets.

Provider |
Secret type |
Improvement |

Alibaba |
alibaba_cloud_access_key_id |
Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. |

AWS |
aws_access_key_id |
Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. |

AWS |
aws_session_token |
Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. |

AWS |
aws_temporary_access_key_id |
Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. |

Google |
google_cloud_storage_access_key_secret |
Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion key identifiers. |

Google |
google_cloud_storage_service_account_access_key_id |
Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. |

Google |
google_cloud_storage_user_access_key_id |
Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. |

OpenVSX |
openvsx_access_token |
Tighten context matching for legacy tokens to avoid treating unrelated UUIDs as credentials. |

Pydantic Services Inc. |
logfire_token |
Match the documented token length and character set to exclude placeholder values and public browser tokens. |

Tencent |
tencent_cloud_secret_id |
Require both letters and digits after the token prefix to exclude alphabetic identifiers such as function names. |

Learn more

Learn more about secret scanning and see the full list of supported secrets in our documentation. Let us know what you think in the community discussion.

items.title: GitHub Copilot weekly releases — November 2
items.lede: This week, Copilot comes to JetBrains Air and Xcode’s coding assistant, with updates to help you manage pull requests, settings, and agent sessions.
items.text:
This week, Copilot comes to JetBrains Air and Xcode’s coding assistant, with updates to help you manage pull requests, settings, and agent sessions.

GitHub Copilot app

- Set up Agent Merge directly from a pull request to have Copilot merge it when it’s ready. It now stays enabled while required checks or rules are pending. You can also check reviewer status, request additional reviews, and select comment text to quote it or discuss it with Copilot.

- Keep working when a conversation reaches its context limit. Compact the conversation or review what’s using the available space directly from the error.

- Start a session by dropping files on “New” in the sidebar. CSV and TSV files now open as tables with sticky headers and an option to view the source.

- Manage sessions in fewer steps. Archive pinned sessions whose pull requests have merged or closed, pin or unpin multiple sessions, and separate nested chats without losing the conversation. My Work now supports more than ten saved custom views.

- Give Copilot guidance on which tool requests to approve without asking you. Personal instructions for assisted approval are opt-in and apply to local sessions.

Install the GitHub Copilot app.

GitHub Copilot CLI

Manage your whole setup in one place. /settings now opens a unified dashboard for your plugins, MCP servers, and more, and you can search across all of your settings.

Install Copilot CLI.

GitHub Copilot in JetBrains

Introducing a new way to use GitHub Copilot in JetBrains IDEs, with Copilot now available in JetBrains Air. Track multiple agent sessions and run tasks locally in your JetBrains IDE or in the cloud through Air Teams, using your existing Copilot subscription.

Get started with Copilot in JetBrains Air.

GitHub Copilot in Xcode

You can now work with GitHub Copilot directly in Xcode’s built-in coding assistant, bringing Copilot into your native Xcode workflow. The integration is now in public preview, available starting with Xcode 27.3 beta.

Get started with Copilot in Xcode.

GitHub Copilot in VS Code (1.145 release)

- Follow the conversation without the clutter or, alternatively, choose to inspect every step. Experimental chat view modes let you collapse or expand reasoning and tool calls without starting a new conversation.

- Check an agent’s work on another machine without leaving VS Code. Preview remote apps and use interactive canvases in the Agents window, now in preview. Enable remote browser support in settings, plus canvases to use that feature.

- Run recurring tasks on a schedule that fits your workflow. Local automations now support cron expressions and custom agents from your workspace.

- Bring screenshots, mockups, and other files into chat without moving them into your workspace. Choose them with Add Context > Files. Cloud sessions only support images.

- Get back into long Copilot chats more smoothly. Past terminal output now renders as you expand or reveal it instead of loading all at once.

Explore everything that’s new in the full release notes.

items.title: Copilot impact dashboard adds chat and VS Code agent usage
items.lede: The Agent adoption chart in the Copilot impact dashboard now includes Copilot Chat and the VS Code Agents window, so you can see engagement across nine Copilot experiences. The adoption cohort called “Passive users” is now “Chat-first users”, which better describes who is in it.
items.text:
The Agent adoption chart in the Copilot impact dashboard now includes Copilot Chat and the VS Code Agents window, so you can see engagement across nine Copilot experiences. The adoption cohort called “Passive users” is now “Chat-first users”, which better describes who is in it. The enterprise and organization 28-day usage metrics reports include the same two features. This builds on feature engagement in the Copilot impact dashboard.

What’s new

- Agent adoption chart: Adds Copilot Chat and the VS Code Agents window, for nine features in total.

- Chat-first users: Replaces the “Passive users” cohort name. These users are active in Copilot but haven’t used a qualifying feature on at least two days in the 28-day period, so they don’t qualify for an adoption phase.

- copilot_feature_engagement.totals_by_feature: Adds chat and vscode_agent entries to enterprise and organization 28-day reports.

Why this matters

Chat is a core Copilot experience, but the dashboard didn’t show it, and users who mainly use chat were labeled passive. Showing Copilot Chat and VS Code Agents window engagement and naming the cohort for what it represents gives a more complete picture of how developers use Copilot.

Important notes

- Adoption phases are unchanged: Chat and the VS Code Agents window are reported as feature engagement but don’t count toward adoption phases. Chat-first users are still the No Cohort value in the API, and cohort sizes don’t change.

- Engagement rule: As with the other features, a user is engaged when they used the feature on at least two days in the 28-day period. A user can be counted under more than one feature. Chat covers Copilot Chat use captured by usage metrics, including agent mode, so users who make agent edits are also counted under chat.

- Scope: Like the other seven features, chat and the VS Code Agents window are only reported in enterprise and organization 28-day reports. Reports for periods before this change only include the original seven features.

- Access: The data is available to enterprise owners and billing managers, organization owners, and anyone with a custom organization or enterprise role that grants the View Copilot Metrics permission. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.

Visit the Copilot impact dashboard documentation and the Copilot usage metrics API documentation to get started.

items.title: Copilot code review: API management and review overview updates
items.lede: You can now manage GitHub Copilot code review settings through the REST and GraphQL APIs, from enterprise policy down to individual repositories. Copilot’s review overview comment is now more compact, and this update includes fixes for billing, automatic reviews, and reliability.
items.text:
You can now manage GitHub Copilot code review settings through the REST and GraphQL APIs, from enterprise policy down to individual repositories. Copilot’s review overview comment is now more compact, and this update includes fixes for billing, automatic reviews, and reliability.

These updates are available to Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans.

🔌 Manage settings and identify Copilot’s output through the API

You can already request reviews, choose their effort level, and get information back through the REST API. You can now also:

- Identify Copilot’s reviews and comments through explicit attribution fields.

- See the review effort a review used, when that metadata is available.

- See which skills, MCP servers, and custom instructions Copilot reported as sources for a comment.

Depending on your role, you can also read and update code review settings:

- Enterprise administrators can enable or disable code review for all organizations, or leave the choice to organization administrators.

- Organization administrators can manage code review enablement, the default review effort, and the runner configuration. Settings your enterprise manages can’t be overridden.

- Repository administrators can manage review effort and whether reviews use custom instructions and MCP tools.

The REST API accepts the same review effort levels as the web interface, and organization and repository settings responses list the levels available to you.

⚠️ The enterprise and organization settings endpoints, including the organization runner endpoint, don’t support GitHub Apps or fine-grained personal access tokens. The repository settings endpoints support both, with Administration: read permission to read settings and Administration: write permission to update them. Classic personal access tokens need repository administrator access.

To get started, see Configuring Copilot code review with the API.

📋 A more compact review overview

New review overviews keep your findings together at the top:

- The review effort used and any surveys move into a compact footer.

- Skipped and content-excluded files share one “Files not reviewed” section, with filenames and linked exclusion reasons.

- Empty sections are left out, and long lists show an overflow count.

You can also tell us what’s wrong with an overview. After you give it a 👎, choose Add a reason and pick the main problem, such as an approval assessment you disagree with, a comment that’s too verbose, or findings that are incorrect or nitpicky. We use this feedback to improve Copilot’s findings.

✨ Other improvements

- Copilot code review agent sessions now show the AI credits consumed in a review.

- The Automatically request Copilot code review repository rule now supports the bypass list, so exempt actors in the list will not receive an automatic review from Copilot.

- Copilot code review organization and repository settings pages have clearer wording and layout.

- On later reviews of the same pull request, findings unrelated to your recent changes are collapsed and then hidden.

- Balanced effort reviews now use three reviewer models, with another model combining their findings.

🐛 Bug fixes

- Billing and preview settings are now preserved when you turn code review off and on again.

- Failed or timed-out reviews are retried once automatically, and Copilot can switch to another eligible model when the preferred one is unavailable.

- GitHub Actions, Dependabot, and apps your organization or enterprise owns can request reviews on bot-authored pull requests again when Block reviews requested with an external Copilot license is on, as long as your organization pays for the review.

- Reviews no longer report a false failure just after starting and discard their results.

- Reviews in progress during a service update now get more time to finish.

- Review surveys no longer appear when your organization has opted out of feedback collection.

items.title: Secret scanning detects secrets in GitHub Actions workflow logs
items.lede: GitHub secret scanning now detects secrets in GitHub Actions workflow logs, in addition to issues, wikis, discussions, and pull requests. Actions workflow log scanning is available in public preview.
items.text:
GitHub secret scanning now detects secrets in GitHub Actions workflow logs, in addition to issues, wikis, discussions, and pull requests. Actions workflow log scanning is available in public preview.

How does Actions workflow log scanning work?

When a workflow run completes, GitHub scans its logs for provider patterns. Findings appear in your repository’s secret scanning alert list, alongside alerts from code and other content, with a link back to the Actions workflow log. Validity checks run for supported secret types, and alerts remain available even after the logs are deleted.

How do I enable it?

The preview is available to enterprises on GitHub Enterprise Cloud with GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Advanced Security, including those with data residency on GHE.com.

Enterprise owners can enable Secret scanning for Actions workflow logs by opening their enterprise settings and selecting Policies, then Advanced Security. Select Enabled in the All repositories dropdown. The policy is disabled by default and applies only to repositories with secret scanning enabled under those licenses.

What should I know about the preview?

Only workflow runs that complete after you enable the feature are scanned; existing logs aren’t backfilled. Generic patterns, custom patterns, AI-detected secrets, and secrets already masked by Actions aren’t detected.

Alerts from Actions workflow logs don’t generate notifications during the preview, so check your repository’s secret scanning alert list directly.

Learn more

Learn more about secret scanning in our product documentation. Have feedback? Let us know by joining the discussion. We’re listening.

items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 in GitHub Copilot
items.lede: Claude Fable 5.2, Anthropic’s newest Fable model, is now generally available in GitHub Copilot. You can use it for complex, multistep coding tasks across large codebases. In early testing, Fable 5.2 solved more tasks than Claude Fable 5.1 while using fewer steps and tool calls.
items.text:
Claude Fable 5.2, Anthropic’s newest Fable model, is now generally available in GitHub Copilot. You can use it for complex, multistep coding tasks across large codebases. In early testing, Fable 5.2 solved more tasks than Claude Fable 5.1 while using fewer steps and tool calls. It also completed hard tasks that earlier models missed.

Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention by default to operate Anthropic’s safety classifiers. Zero data retention access is available for certain eligible enterprise customers. Continue reading for more details.

This model is billed at provider list pricing under usage-based billing. See Models and pricing for GitHub Copilot for details.

Availability in GitHub Copilot

Claude Fable 5.2 is available to Copilot Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise users. You can select the model in the model picker in:

- Visual Studio Code

- Visual Studio

- Copilot CLI

- GitHub Copilot coding agent

- GitHub Copilot app

- github.com

- GitHub Mobile on iOS and Android

- JetBrains IDEs

- Xcode

- Eclipse

Rollout will be gradual. Check back soon if you don’t see it yet.

Enabling access

Copilot Enterprise and Copilot Business plan administrators must enable the Claude Fable 5.2 policy in Copilot settings. The policy is off by default.

Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention by default. When Claude Fable 5.2 is used, Anthropic retains data, including prompts and outputs, to operate safety classifiers that detect harmful use. Retained data is not used to train Anthropic’s models. Other Claude models, except for Fable 5, Fable 5.1, and Fable 5.2, continue to operate under zero data retention (ZDR).

To learn more, see Anthropic’s data retention practices for Mythos-class models. Enabling the Claude Fable 5.2 policy constitutes acknowledgment of this requirement. Leaving it off keeps Claude Fable 5.2 unavailable to your organization.

Zero data retention access for eligible enterprises

Eligible customers can use Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Fable 5 with zero data retention through the end of the calendar year under a time-bound exemption while Anthropic rolls out Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS). After that point, continued use of the models will require EFS, which will enable automated safety monitoring while also giving eligible customers more options for how their data is retained. This includes the option to use storage and encryption keys under their own control. Between now and then we will be working with Anthropic to provide feedback on EFS.

If your enterprise is approved for access, Claude Fable 5.2, Fable 5.1, and Fable 5 requests will be routed to zero data retention endpoints when the model is enabled. To learn whether your organization qualifies, contact your GitHub account team. GitHub Support cannot determine eligibility or enable access.

Approval will not automatically enable the models. After approval, a Copilot Enterprise or Copilot Business administrator must still enable the Claude Fable 5.2 policy in Copilot settings.

Learn more

To explore all models available in GitHub Copilot, see our documentation on models and get started with Copilot.

items.text:
Since the new dashboard experience became the default, we’ve heard from developers that it used too much space to show too little. Generous padding, wrapped titles, and a low default item count meant extra navigation just to see what needed attention. items.title: C++ language server now auto-configures MSBuild builds
items.lede: The Microsoft C++ Language Server for GitHub Copilot CLI now bundles its MSBuild compile commands extractor and invokes it automatically. An agent no longer needs to discover and run a separate configuration skill before it can get precise code intelligence for your project.
items.text:
The Microsoft C++ Language Server for GitHub Copilot CLI now bundles its MSBuild compile commands extractor and invokes it automatically. An agent no longer needs to discover and run a separate configuration skill before it can get precise code intelligence for your project. For more information, including the installation instructions, see the main repository page.

What changed

Previously, setting up go-to-definition, find references, and other language server features for an MSBuild-based C++ project required you to either provide your own compile_commands.json file or Copilot to locate and run a configuration skill before it could generate a compilation database. That extra discovery step added setup time and consumed tokens before Copilot could start working with your code.

Now:

- The compile commands extractor is bundled directly with the C++ language server, so it’s always available.

- Copilot invokes the extractor when starting the language server on project open, with no manual or agent-driven setup skill required.

- Compilation database generation for MSBuild projects is deterministic, reducing setup token usage.

Configure other build systems

For other build systems, you can provide your own compile_commands.json or use a skill to generate one:

- For CMake projects, use the generate compile commands skill introduced in the earlier C++ language server release by asking Copilot CLI to “load project.”

- For custom build systems, follow the guide to create a custom build extractor skill.

Get started

Follow the Microsoft C++ Language Server quick start to install the plugin and accept the EULA. If your repository contains an MSBuild-based C++ project, Copilot will automatically generate the compilation database it needs for accurate code intelligence.

An active GitHub Copilot subscription is required.

Help improve the Microsoft C++ Language Server by completing the C++ language server survey. To report a problem or suggest an improvement, open an issue in the Microsoft C++ Language Server repository.

items.title: Dependabot alerts will pause on inactive repositories
items.lede: Starting December 8, 2026, GitHub will turn off Dependabot alerts on most repositories with no activity in the past year. Their existing alerts are archived, not deleted, and you can restore them at any time.
items.text:
Starting December 8, 2026, GitHub will turn off Dependabot alerts on most repositories with no activity in the past year. Their existing alerts are archived, not deleted, and you can restore them at any time. With vulnerability discovery and alert volume growing quickly, this keeps Dependabot fast and reliable for the repositories you’re actively developing.

What counts as activity

GitHub counts any of these as activity:

- Pushing to any branch or tag

- Creating the repository

- Turning on Dependabot alerts

Turn alerts back on

Any push to the repository automatically turns Dependabot alerts back on. You can also turn them on in the repository’s settings. Either way, GitHub restores the archived alerts, and the one-year clock starts over.

Keep alerts on regardless of activity

GitHub won’t turn off alerts on repositories with an enforced security configuration that enables Dependabot alerts. It also skips repositories in enterprises whose Dependabot alerts policy doesn’t allow repository administrators to enable or disable alerts.

This change applies to all plans on github.com and to GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. For data residency customers, archived alerts are stored in the same region as the rest of your enterprise’s data. It doesn’t apply to GitHub Enterprise Server.

items.title: Issue types and fields are available for personal accounts
items.lede: Issue types and issue fields are now generally available on repositories owned by personal accounts. This brings the same planning capabilities to individual developers and open source maintainers to standardize your workflows and organize issues across repositories.
items.text:
Issue types and issue fields are now generally available on repositories owned by personal accounts. This brings the same planning capabilities to individual developers and open source maintainers to standardize your workflows and organize issues across repositories.

Get started with issue types and issue fields

- Customize issue types: You can customize issue types from your personal account settings on the Issue types page under “Planning”. The defaults are Bug, Task, and Feature. You can customize them and create up to 25 issue types.

- Customize issue fields: You can customize issue fields from your personal account settings on the Issue fields page under “Planning”. The default issue fields are Priority, Effort, Start date, and Target date. You can customize them and create up to 25 issue fields, with support for text, number, date, single-select, and multi-select fields. You can also pin fields to issue types or make them available on issues without a type.

- Apply them to issues: You can set the issue type and fields when creating an issue or viewing an existing issue. You can also use them in projects to create custom views and perform bulk updates.

- Use the API to automate: You can use the REST and GraphQL APIs and webhooks to programmatically manage issue types and fields.

Learn more about managing issue types and managing issue fields.

Create labels and milestones from an issue

You can now create labels and milestones directly from an issue, without navigating to the repository’s labels or milestones pages. If a label or milestone doesn’t match your search criteria, you’ll be prompted to create one.

items.title: Manage AI Scan for repositories using the REST API
items.lede: You can now turn GitHub code scanning’s AI Scan for repositories on or off with the REST API at the organization and repository levels. This public preview adds a repository_scan setting to the existing AI Scan enablement endpoints.
items.text:
You can now turn GitHub code scanning’s AI Scan for repositories on or off with the REST API at the organization and repository levels. This public preview adds a repository_scan setting to the existing AI Scan enablement endpoints. You can roll out AI Scan for repositories with scripts and infrastructure as code instead of changing settings one organization or repository at a time.

Manage AI Scan for repositories at scale

Set the repository_scan property to enabled or disabled on the AI Scan enablement endpoints:

- GET and PATCH /orgs/{org}/code-scanning/ai-scan

- GET and PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/code-scanning/ai-scan

The setting works the same way as the existing pr_scan setting for AI Scan for pull requests:

- When an organization disables AI Scan for repositories, its repositories can’t enable it

- When an organization enables it, its repositories inherit the setting and can opt out individually

- When an enterprise policy doesn’t allow AI Scan, requests to enable it return a 422 error

You can update pr_scan and repository_scan in the same request. If either change is blocked, the request returns a 422 error and neither setting changes.

Turning on AI Scan for repositories doesn’t start a scan. Users with write access still run scans on demand, and each scan consumes GitHub Code Security AI credits.

Who can use it

Organization owners and security managers can manage the organization setting. Repository administrators can opt individual repositories out. AI Scan for repositories is available for public repositories owned by organizations and for private or internal repositories with GitHub Code Security or GitHub Advanced Security. Enterprise owners must first allow AI Scan in the enterprise policy. GitHub Enterprise Server isn’t supported.

To get started, see REST API endpoints for code scanning and AI Scan for a repository’s backlog.
